articles.title: Watch: US man struck by lightning describes 'horrific' experience
articles.summary: Thomas Fahmy says he saw "a bright white flash" and instantly fell to the ground.
articles.body:

Thomas Fahmy said he had been walking to the dentist on 27 August when he saw "a bright white flash" and instantly fell to the ground.

"I've never felt these sensations ever in my life", he told CBS News, BBC News's US partner.

articles.title: Prefeitura divulga lista final com 1 mil vagas para professores na BA | G1
articles.standfirst: Lista com os nomes dos candidatos está disponível no Diário Oficial do Município.
articles.summary: Lista com os nomes dos candidatos está disponível no Diário Oficial do Município.
articles.body:
Divulgado resultado de concurso para professor em Feira de Santana — Foto: Divulgação

A Prefeitura de Feira de Santana , segunda maior cidade da Bahia, publicou, nesta quinta-feira (3), a lista final de candidatos aprovados do concurso público que oferece 1 mil vagas imediatas para professores da rede municipal de ensino. A lista com os nomes dos candidatos está disponível no Diário Oficial do Município. [Clique aqui para conferir a relação completa].

As vagas são destinadas ao quadro efetivo da rede municipal de ensino. Além das oportunidades imediatas, o concurso também prevê formação de cadastro reserva.

A relação dos candidatos consta no anexo único do edital de homologação publicado no Diário Oficial.

Também há vagas para professores das áreas de artes, educação física, história, geografia, ciências, matemática, língua inglesa e língua portuguesa.

O salário inicial previsto no edital é de R$ 5.212,34, para uma jornada de 40 horas semanais.

As provas objetivas e discursivas foram realizadas em 8 de março de 2026. O concurso também contou com prova de títulos, de caráter classificatório.

A homologação do resultado final encerra a etapa de seleção prevista no edital e confirma oficialmente o resultado do concurso.

articles.title: Vereador morre após ser arremessado de lancha em acidente em rio do AM | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo relatos obtidos pela Rede Amazônica, Edgar Júnior estava sentado na parte dianteira da embarcação, que era aberta. Com o impacto da batida, ele teria sido lançado para a frente.
articles.summary: O vereador Edgar Júnior, de Alvarães, morreu após ser arremessado de uma lancha no Rio Solimões; a embarcação transportava nove pessoas, incluindo um deputado estadual.
articles.body:
Vereador de Alvarães Edgar Litaiff Mendes Júnior — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

O vereador de Alvarães Edgar Litaiff Mendes Junior ( União Brasil ), conhecido como "Edgarzinho", morreu após ser arremessado de uma lancha que bateu em um banco de areia no Rio Solimões, próximo ao município, no interior do Amazonas. O acidente aconteceu por volta das 22h de quarta-feira (2), quando o grupo retornava de Uarini para Alvarães.

Segundo relatos obtidos pela Rede Amazônica , Edgar Júnior estava sentado na parte dianteira da embarcação, que era aberta . Com o impacto da batida, ele teria sido lançado para a frente. Ainda conforme o relato, a lancha continuou em movimento e passou sobre o vereador.

O corpo foi levado para Alvarães e encaminhado ao hospital do município, mas Edgar já estava sem vida.

A lancha transportava nove pessoas . A Rede Amazônica apurou que os outros ocupantes da comitiva não ficaram feridos .

Entre os passageiros estava o deputado estadual Thiago Abrahim (MDB). O parlamentar havia participado de uma agenda em Alvarães e, depois, seguiu para Uarini.

Após o acidente, Thiago permaneceu em Alvarães. Segundo a equipe do deputado, ele está bem e não sofreu ferimentos.

Em nota divulgada na manhã desta quinta-feira (3), o parlamentar lamentou a morte do vereador e informou que a agenda de campanha foi suspensa. ( Confira a nota na íntegra ao final desta reportagem ).

Edgar Litaiff Mendes Junior, conhecido como Edgar Júnior, era natural de Alvarães. Segundo informações declaradas à Justiça Eleitoral, ele trabalhava como agente administrativo e tinha ensino médio incompleto.

Nas eleições municipais de 2024, disputou pela primeira vez uma vaga na Câmara Municipal de Alvarães. Candidato pelo União Brasil, concorreu com o nome de urna "Edgarzinho" e recebeu 349 votos, o equivalente a 3,37% dos votos válidos.

Ele foi eleito pelo quociente partidário e terminou a eleição como o sexto vereador mais votado do município.

Prefeitura, Câmara e deputado lamentam morte

A Prefeitura de Alvarães e a Câmara Municipal lamentaram a morte do vereador. Em nota, a prefeitura destacou que Edgar Júnior atuou com "ética e compromisso" em prol do desenvolvimento da cidade e prestou solidariedade aos familiares e amigos.

Já a Câmara, por meio do presidente Valdinei Cardenes e dos demais vereadores, manifestou pesar pela perda e desejou força à família neste momento de luto.

Em nota divulgada na manhã desta quinta-feira (3), o deputado Thiago Abrahim lamentou a morte do vereador, que integrava a comitiva da viagem, e informou que todos os compromissos da agenda foram suspensos.

A equipe do parlamentar afirmou ainda que está à disposição da família e das autoridades para colaborar com o esclarecimento das circunstâncias do acidente.

articles.title: Aeroporto de Feira de Santana tem atividades suspensas temporariamente | G1
articles.standfirst: Interrupção ocorreu após fiscalização da Secretaria Municipal de Meio Ambiente. Órgão constatou que a licença do local venceu em dezembro de 2025.
articles.summary: Interrupção ocorreu após fiscalização da Secretaria Municipal de Meio Ambiente. Órgão constatou que a licença do local venceu em dezembro de 2025.
articles.body:
Aeroporto de Feira de Santana — Foto: Reprodução | Prefeitura Municipal de Feira de Santana

O Aeroporto de Feira de Santana , segunda maior cidade da Bahia, teve as atividades suspensas temporariamente na quarta-feira (2), após uma fiscalização da Secretaria Municipal de Meio Ambiente. Segundo o órgão, a licença ambiental do empreendimento está vencida desde dezembro de 2025 e o pedido de renovação ainda não havia sido protocolado.

A fiscalização também identificou o descumprimento de condicionantes ambientais previstas na licença anterior. Diante das irregularidades, a secretaria determinou a suspensão das atividades até que a situação seja regularizada.

A medida tem caráter preventivo e temporário. De acordo com a Secretaria Municipal de Meio Ambiente, o aeroporto só poderá retomar as atividades após a empresa cumprir as obrigações apontadas pela fiscalização e regularizar o licenciamento ambiental junto ao órgão competente.

As normas ambientais são exigências estabelecidas pelo órgão responsável pelo licenciamento para acompanhar e controlar possíveis impactos causados pelo empreendimento. Elas podem envolver, por exemplo, monitoramento, manutenção, gerenciamento de resíduos e controle de riscos.

Segundo a secretaria, o cumprimento dessas medidas é necessário para garantir que o empreendimento esteja funcionando de acordo com as normas ambientais.

A secretária municipal de Meio Ambiente, Jaciara Costa, afirmou que a suspensão faz parte dos procedimentos adotados em casos de irregularidades.

Ainda conforme a pasta, a responsabilidade pela manutenção da licença ambiental válida e pelo cumprimento das condicionantes é da empresa responsável pelo empreendimento.

O g1 procurou a administração do Aeroporto de Feira de Santana sobre o ocorrido e aguarda o retorno.

articles.title: Entenda os sinais de desconforto ou dor no pets | G1
articles.standfirst: Veterinária explica que, além da dor, sinais de desconforto também podem estar relacionados a mudanças no comportamento dos animais. Em Itapetininga (SP), tutoras compartilham como ficam atentas a comportamentos incomuns nos pets.
articles.summary: O comportamento de um pet pode indicar mudanças de humor e até mesmo algo que esteja o incomodando. Mas sabia que um animal também pode apresentar se estiver doente?
articles.body:
O comportamento de um pet pode revelar mudanças de humor, preferências em relação ao ambiente e até indicar que algo não está bem. Mas você sabia que os animais também podem apresentar sinais de dor ou doença mesmo sem sintomas aparentes?

Para explicar como identificar esses sinais e entender melhor o comportamento dos pets, o g1 conversou com a médica veterinária Giovanna Del Cistia, de Sorocaba (SP), que apontou quais mudanças devem chamar a atenção dos tutores e deu orientações sobre como agir nesses casos.

Ao g1, a veterinária de Sorocaba explicou quais podem ser os sinais de desconforto apresentado pelos animais — Foto: Arquivo pessoal/Maria Carolina Sanches

A profissional apontou que um dos sinais mais sutis, e que muitas vezes não é percebido pelos tutores como um indicativo de dor, é a redução do apetite e da agitação dos pets.

“Um animal pode dormir mais,ficar mais apegado ao tutor ou então até mais agressivo, e por vezes evitando usar alguma parte do corpo”, listou.

A veterinária explicou também que a dor ativa mecanismos de defesa no organismo dos animais, o que favorece o estresse crônico. Por causa disso, o pet muda a forma que interage com o ambiente.

“Animais com dor tendem a ter uma frequência cardíaca e respiratória um pouco mais elevada. Além da dor, sinais de desconforto também podem estar ligados a fatores comportamentais, como estresse”, disse a especialista.

Giovanna Del Cistia é veterinária e mora em Sorocaba (SP) — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

A lambedura excessiva das patas ou de alguma parte do corpo também é um sinal de alerta. No caso dos gatos, um dos comportamentos apresentados é urinar com frequência fora da caixinha de areia.

“Muitas vezes os sinais são sutis ou os tutores não conseguem interpretar aquele comportamento como um possível sinal de dor”, reforçou a veterinária.

Veterinária explica quais são os sinais que um pet apresenta ao sentir dor — Foto: Arquivo pessoal/Stephany Marcondes

Essas mudanças de comportamento podem ocorrer em pets de qualquer idade. No entanto, Giovanna alerta que os animais idosos são mais suscetíveis a dores crônicas, como as causadas pela artrose.

“O animal idoso saudável, apesar de ter menos energia que um filhote ou adulto, ainda deve se movimentar e comer normalmente. Animais idosos muito prostrados podem estar apresentando dores”, completou.

Por fim, a profissional orienta os tutores a procurar um médico veterinário ao perceber qualquer mudança de comportamento ou reação diferente do habitual no pet.

“Nem todo sinal de desconforto é dor e nem todo analgésico humano pode ser usado em animais, além de cães e gatos necessitarem de dosagens específicas. Portanto, a indicação é sempre levar à um veterinário”, reforçou ao g1 .

É importante observar diariamente se a alimentação e a ingestão de líquidos estão normais e se o pet apresenta alguma mudança de comportamento ou de humor.

Na casa de Stephany Marcondes, de 25 anos, tutora de Pandora e Biggu, observar os sinais apresentados pelos animais faz parte da rotina.

“Acho importante observar o comportamento deles no dia a dia, porque muitas vezes eles demonstram que alguma coisa não está bem mesmo sem apresentar sinais muito evidentes”, relatou à reportagem.

Em Itapetininga, Stephany é tutora de 'Bigu' que tem três anos — Foto: Arquivo pessoal/Stephany Marcondes

Ao perceber alguma mudança, a tutora busca entender se aconteceu algo de diferente no dia do pet ou da família.

“Quando estão desconfortáveis, geralmente ficam mais ofegantes e irritados. Quando estão doentes, ficam mais quietinhos, desanimados e perdem o interesse em brincar. Já quando estão com medo ou inseguros, costumam procurar um lugar para se esconder e podem ficar tremendo”, apontou a tutora.

Stephany é tutora de dois cães e disse ao g1 sempre ficar atenta às mudanças no comportamento — Foto: Arquivo pessoal/Stephany Marcondes

“Hoje consigo identificar alguns sinais apenas pela mudança de comportamento. Quando percebo que estão ofegantes sem terem feito esforço ou muito quietinhos e sem vontade de brincar, já fico em alerta porque sei que provavelmente existe alguma coisa diferente acontecendo”, completou.

Stephany conta que os cães conseguem demonstrar quando algo está incomodando. Segundo ela, a cadela é mais expressiva e consegue mostrar o que quer e o que está sentindo, seja pelo olhar ou pela maneira como age.

“O Biggu já é mais tranquilo e reservado, mas também percebo que ele tem a própria maneira de se comunicar comigo. Com o tempo, convivendo com eles, a gente acaba aprendendo a interpretar pequenas mudanças e entender melhor o que cada um está tentando demonstrar”, esclareceu.

Ao g1 , a fisioterapeuta Maria Carolina Sanches, de 27 anos, disse que fica atenta aos comportamento de seu gato Draco, que tem seis anos.

“O Draco é extremamente expressivo, é fácil saber quando ele está incomodado com alguma coisa ou até mesmo com alguém”, relatou a tutora.

Maria Sanches, moradora de Itapetininga, é tutora do gato apelidado de Draco — Foto: Arquivo pessoal/Maria Sanches

Ela relembrou um caso em que o pet machucou a parte interna da orelha, mas o ferimento não era visível. Mesmo sem apresentar sintomas aparentes, o animal mostrou à tutora que algo estava diferente do normal por meio de miados repetitivos.

“Seja por miado e pela tonalidade dos miados, quanto pela forma como ela dá mordidinhas no meu tornozelo, eu já consigo entender o que ele tá querendo”, contou Maria.

Um dos comportamentos que os gatos podem apresentar é urinar com frequência fora da caixa de areia — Foto: Arquivo pessoal/Maria Sanches

A fisioterapeuta relatou que, como o pet gosta muito de ficar brincando no sol e deitado no quintal, quando Draco passa mais tempo dentro de casa, ela fica em alerta para observar se há algum de errado com o animal.

“Ele gosta bastante de brincar no sol ou de ficar deitado no quintal, se ele fica muito dentro de casa a gente já começa a achar estranho, principalmente se fica muito tempo quieto ou soltando uns miados baixos resmungando”, concluiu.

À reportagem, ela contou que sempre fica atenta às mudanças do animal, pois ele é expressivo — Foto: Arquivo pessoal/Maria Carolina Sanches

articles.title: Em áudio, ex-número 3 da Fazenda de SP fala em comprar sauna para lavar dinheiro e teme ser algemado | G1
articles.standfirst: Gravação de almoço entre fiscais foi encontrada no celular de outro investigado e passou por perícia. André Weiss, preso nesta quinta, também aparece discutindo o 'rateio' de valores relacionados a processos tributários.
articles.summary: Gravação de almoço entre fiscais foi encontrada no celular de outro investigado e passou por perícia. André Weiss, preso nesta quinta, também aparece discutindo o 'rateio' de valores relacionados a processos tributários.
articles.body:
O ex-diretor-geral da Administração Tributária de São Paulo André Weiss, preso nesta quinta-feira (3) por suspeita de envolvimento em um esquema de corrupção na Secretaria da Fazenda , afirmou durante um almoço entre fiscais que pensou em comprar uma sauna para lavar dinheiro.

A conversa foi gravada em julho de 2023 por um dos participantes e encontrada posteriormente pelo Ministério Público de São Paulo (MPSP) no celular do auditor fiscal Artur Gomes da Silva Neto, preso na Operação Ícaro, em agosto de 2025.

Segundo a transcrição apresentada pelo MPSP, Weiss também demonstrou preocupação com a possibilidade de chamar a atenção das autoridades caso aparecesse dirigindo uma Mercedes de R$ 250 mil. Ele afirmou que isso poderia levá-lo aos jornais e fazê-lo terminar algemado.

Weiss ocupou até maio deste ano o terceiro posto mais alto na hierarquia da Secretaria da Fazenda, subordinado apenas ao subsecretário da Receita Estadual e ao secretário da Fazenda. Para o MPSP, ele comandava o núcleo público da organização criminosa investigada.

Em um dos trechos da gravação, Weiss sugere que uma sauna seria um bom negócio para receber valores em espécie:

“Você sabe que eu pensei em pegar dinheiro e comprar uma sauna em São Paulo... pra fazer reunião... vamos juntar uma grana e vamos pegar uma porra de uma sauna, né? E para lavar também é bom”, afirmou.

Na sequência, ele argumentou que os clientes dificilmente utilizariam cartões no estabelecimento:

“Quantas pessoas entram em sauna e pagam em dinheiro? Quase todas, cara.” “Pô, quem que vai passar um cartão em sauna? Ninguém”, prosseguiu.

O MPSP afirma que a fala descreve, em primeira pessoa, uma possível forma de lavagem de dinheiro por meio de um estabelecimento com grande circulação de recursos em espécie. Os documentos não indicam que a compra da sauna tenha sido concretizada.

Em outro momento do almoço, Weiss disse que era preciso ter cuidado com demonstrações externas de riqueza.

“Se eu comprar uma Mercedes... eu não vou comprar uma Mercedes seminova... 250 pau uma Mercedes, né... se você aparece na Delegacia, cara... isso aí vai sair no jornal”, afirmou.

Em seguida, acrescentou: “Você é algemado... chega um promotor pra me prender na hora lá.”

A conversa ocorreu em 27 de julho de 2023, menos de um mês antes da primeira entrega de propina relatada pelo ex-delegado regional tributário do Butantã Paulo Sérgio Siqueira Prado, que firmou um acordo de colaboração premiada.

O áudio, com mais de duas horas de duração, foi submetido a uma perícia do Núcleo de Computação Forense do Centro de Apoio Operacional à Execução (Caex), que atestou sua integridade.

A Justiça considerou que a gravação pode ser usada como prova por ter sido feita por um dos participantes da conversa, sem atuação clandestina dos investigadores.

Paulo Sérgio Siqueira do Prado, conhecido como "PP", se aposentou em 2024, mas durante a carreira na secretaria, ocupou cargos de destaque na Receita Estadual de São Paulo. — Foto: Montagem/g1/Reprodução/Redes Sociais

Durante o almoço, os fiscais também discutiram procedimentos de ressarcimento de ICMS de grandes redes varejistas.

Ao ser questionado sobre o assunto de uma reunião reservada que teria mantido com Paulo Prado, Weiss respondeu: “Rateio”.

Em outros trechos, eles falam sobre três processos cujos números ou valores “não estariam batendo” e combinam um novo encontro para discutir o assunto.

Segundo o MPSP, o conteúdo indica que os participantes tratavam da divisão de vantagens indevidas relacionadas à liberação dos créditos tributários. A gravação também apresenta relatos e piadas sobre “caixinhas” mantidas por fiscais.

A decisão que decretou a prisão preventiva afirma que o áudio ganha relevância quando analisado em conjunto com a colaboração premiada, documentos manuscritos sobre a divisão dos valores, dados bancários e relatórios de inteligência financeira.

Paulo Prado declarou ter recebido aproximadamente R$ 13,6 milhões do advogado João André Buttini de Moraes para agilizar e destravar pedidos de ressarcimento tributário.

Segundo o colaborador, cerca de R$ 4,5 milhões foram posteriormente repassados a Weiss. As entregas teriam ocorrido em dinheiro vivo, dentro de mochilas, principalmente em restaurantes da Rua Ferreira de Araújo e em uma unidade da Ofner na Rua Pedroso de Moraes, em Pinheiros.

Prado também afirmou que, a partir de meados de 2023, passou a pagar R$ 250 mil mensais a Weiss para ser mantido à frente da Delegacia Regional Tributária do Butantã até sua aposentadoria, ocorrida em 2024.

O MPSP afirma ter encontrado na casa de Prado documentos manuscritos com divisões de valores. Uma das anotações atribui a “Weiss” uma cota de R$ 747,1 mil relacionada a um processo da Via.

O juiz responsável pelo caso ressaltou que as acusações não estão baseadas somente na palavra do colaborador. Segundo ele, há elementos externos de corroboração, como documentos, quebras de sigilo, movimentações financeiras e a gravação ambiental periciada.

Weiss e Buttini foram presos preventivamente nesta quinta. Outros seis agentes públicos foram afastados das funções e estão proibidos de acessar as dependências e os sistemas da Secretaria da Fazenda.

Os investigados poderão responder por organização criminosa, corrupção ativa e passiva e lavagem de dinheiro.

O g1 procurou as defesas de André Weiss e dos demais investigados citados, além da Secretaria da Fazenda, e aguarda retorno. O espaço permanece aberto.

Desde a deflagração da Operação Ícaro, em agosto de 2025, a Secretaria da Fazenda e Planejamento atua em conjunto com o Ministério Público de São Paulo na apuração rigorosa dos fatos. As ações da pasta resultaram na demissão de cinco envolvidos, além de um exonerado e 17 servidores afastados sem remuneração.

As empresas envolvidas também estão sendo responsabilizadas, com autuações específicas que já resultaram na constituição de mais de R$ 3 bilhões em créditos tributários, multas e juros.

Qualquer novo fato decorrente dos desdobramentos da operação, inclusive de eventuais acordos de delação ou denúncias, será rigorosamente apurado e, comprovadas irregularidades, serão adotadas as medidas cabíveis.

A Secretaria colabora integralmente com as investigações e reafirma seu compromisso com a rigorosa apuração e responsabilização de eventuais desvios, sem qualquer tolerância com condutas irregulares.

articles.title: Quote of the day by Jeff Bezos: “I knew that if I failed I wouldn’t regret that, but…” - a lesson about risk, failure and regret
articles.summary: Tech News News: There are decisions that become difficult precisely because both choices carry a cost. Staying where things are familiar can offer security, while tak.
articles.body: There are decisions that become difficult precisely because both choices carry a cost. Staying where things are familiar can offer security, while taking a chance can leave a person facing an outcome that cannot be predicted. Jeff Bezos encountered that dilemma in the 1990s, when he was working at the investment firm D. E. Shaw began considering an idea built around the rapidly expanding internet. Leaving a well-paid job for an online bookseller was hardly a guaranteed route to success. Bezos knew the business could fail. What mattered to him was a different possibility: that years later, he might look back and wish he had given the idea a chance. He eventually left his job and founded Amazon. The decision became one of the defining moments of his career, but the reasoning behind it came before anyone knew how the company would turn out.Quote of the day by Jeff Bezos“I knew that if I failed I wouldn’t regret that, but I knew the one thing I might regret is not trying.”What Jeff Bezos meant by the quoteBezos was describing the way he weighed the risk of leaving his established career. He did not know whether Amazon would succeed. In fact, he considered failure a realistic possibility.His thinking centred on regret rather than prediction. He imagined himself much older and considered how he might view the decision with the benefit of hindsight. If the business failed, he would at least know that he had attempted it. If he stayed in his job and never tried, there would be no answer to the question of what might have happened.The quote is therefore not simply about being unafraid of failure. It is about recognising that inaction can also have consequences. Sometimes the safest decision in the short term can leave a person with a longer-lasting question.The modest beginnings behind a much bigger companyIt is easy to view the original Amazon through the scale of the company that exists today. That can distort what Bezos was actually deciding in 1994.Amazon did not begin as a plan to create a vast technology and retail company. It began as an online bookstore. The first version of the business was focused on selling books through a website at a time when buying something online was still unfamiliar to most people.The company opened its virtual doors in July 1995.Within its first weeks, Amazon had shipped books across the United States and to customers overseas. The catalogue also gave the business an advantage that physical shops struggled to match. It could offer a huge range of titles without having to keep every book on shelves.The early success did not prove that Bezos had known what would happen. It showed what happened after he decided to try.The long-term view behind a risky choiceThe phrase most closely associated with Bezos's decision is his “regret minimisation framework”.Rather than trying to predict every detail of the future, he imagined reaching old age and looking back at the choice. From that imagined future perspective, he considered which decision was more likely to cause regret. The framework simplified the problem. If Amazon failed, Bezos could return to the job market and continue with his career. If he never tried, he might spend years wondering whether the business could have worked.It was not a mathematical formula. It was a way of changing the time frame of the decision. A difficult choice in the present can look different when viewed from decades later.Why failure mattered less to him than uncertaintyFailure produces an answer. If a business closes, a person knows that a particular approach did not work. If an application is rejected, there is a definite outcome. Even an unsuccessful project can reveal what needs to change.Not trying provides none of that. The possibility remains hypothetical. There is no evidence showing whether the idea could have succeeded or failed.For Bezos, that unresolved possibility was harder to accept than failure itself. That is perhaps the most precise way to understand the quote. He was not claiming that failure feels good. He was saying that failure was an outcome he could live with, while never making the attempt might leave a question that could not be settled.A lesson about decisions rather than ambitionThe quote can be applied without turning every difficult choice into an entrepreneurial gamble. A person considering a career change, a new qualification, a business idea or a creative project might ask a similar question: which outcome would be harder to live with years from now?Sometimes the responsible decision is to stay put. Financial obligations, family circumstances, timing and the consequences of failure all matter. Bezos's framework cannot account for every situation.What it can do is introduce another consideration into the decision, the cost of never finding out.Trying can be smaller than people thinkThere is also no need for “trying” to involve quitting a job or risking a life's savings.It might mean testing an idea on a small scale. Applying for an opportunity. Taking a course. Speaking to someone in an industry you are considering. Building a first version of a project before deciding whether to pursue it seriously.Those steps can reduce uncertainty without requiring an immediate leap. In that sense, the useful part of Bezos's thinking is not necessarily the size of the risk he took. It is the way he separated the fear of failure from the question of future regret.Lessons to learn from Jeff Bezos’ quoteFailure is not always the worst outcomeConsider the cost of inactionThink beyond the present momentRegret can be a useful decision-making toolTrying does not always mean taking a huge riskDo not confuse uncertainty with failureSecurity has a cost tooA decision does not need a guaranteed outcome to be worthwhileLearn to separate fear from judgementThe goal is not to avoid every mistakeGet the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: A 5,000-acre Wyoming ranch was bought by conservationists in the 1990s; instead of ending ranching, they kept cattle grazing to protect the ecosystem
articles.summary: US News: When conservationists bought a Wyoming cattle ranch in the 1990s, most people assumed the herds would disappear. Instead, they discovered something su.
articles.body: When conservationists bought a Wyoming cattle ranch in the 1990s, most people assumed the herds would disappear. Instead, they discovered something surprising: keeping cattle on the land, managed carefully, could actually protect it. This is the story of Red Canyon Ranch near Lander, Wyoming, purchased by The Nature Conservancy as an experiment in coexistence between ranching and wildlife. Rather than retiring the pastures, the organisation kept roughly 600 head of cattle grazing across the property, using science to test whether livestock and native ecosystems could genuinely thrive together. Decades later, the ranch stands as a working case study in adaptive land management, one that continues to shape how conservation groups across the American West think about grazing, biodiversity, and the future of working lands.How a Wyoming ranch proved cattle grazing could save an ecosystem, not destroy itIn the early 1990s, The Nature Conservancy acquired Red Canyon Ranch, a roughly 35,000-acre spread near Lander, Wyoming, made up of about 5,000 deeded acres alongside tens of thousands of leased federal acres. The purchase was unusual for its time. Rather than converting the property into an untouched nature preserve, the organization chose to keep it operating as a working cattle ranch. This decision reflected a broader shift within the conservation world during the era, one that questioned whether removing all human activity was truly the best path to protecting fragile landscapes, or whether carefully managed use could sometimes do the job just as well.Why grazing stayed part of the planCattle didn't stay on Red Canyon Ranch out of sentiment, the reasoning was ecological. For thousands of years, grazing animals had shaped Wyoming's sagebrush steppe and grasslands, starting with bison and other native herbivores that roamed the land long before ranching existed. Pull large grazers out entirely, and you don't necessarily get a healthier landscape; you risk disrupting processes the ecosystem has come to depend on. So the Conservancy took a different route: using cattle to stand in for that lost grazing pressure, moving herds through rotational and adaptive patterns designed to echo how wild grazers once used the land. This approach aimed to maintain healthy grasslands, support diverse plant communities, and avoid the overgrazing that had damaged other Western rangelands throughout the twentieth century.Balancing wildlife, water, and working landHowever, the rationale for cattle grazing at the Red Canyon Ranch was based on ecology, not emotions. Large grazers have been a part of the sagebrush steppe and grasslands of Wyoming for thousands of years, first in the form of bison and other native herbivores. Complete elimination of grazing from the area, experts argued, would not be a restoration but an interference into the natural processes. Hence, The Conservancy used cattle to emulate the historical pattern of grazing with the use of rotational and adaptive grazing techniques. The ongoing presence of a working herd meant researchers could gather real, long-term data on how grazing intensity and timing affected the broader ecosystem.A model that still shapes conservation todayRed Canyon Ranch helped popularize a strategy now used on conservation properties across the West: keeping agriculture and biodiversity goals aligned rather than treating them as opposites. The approach has since informed similar projects on other working ranches, where conservation groups partner with ranchers instead of buying them out entirely. It hasn't been without debate, since some critics argue that any grazing carries ecological costs compared with fully rested land. Still, the ranch's decades-long track record offers real evidence that thoughtfully managed livestock operations can coexist with wildlife conservation, offering a template for balancing food production, rural livelihoods, and ecosystem health.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Swollen river below, unfinished bridge above: Chhattisgarh kids brave raging water to reach school
articles.summary: RAIPUR: School bag on back. Feet on a slippery iron ladder. A swollen river 20 feet below. For children in Mainpur block of Chhattisgarh's Gariyaband .
articles.body: RAIPUR: School bag on back. Feet on a slippery iron ladder. A swollen river 20 feet below. For children in Mainpur block of Chhattisgarh's Gariyaband district, about 190km southeast of Raipur, this is a daily commute to school when monsoon turns the normally shallow Pairi river into a torrent.Dozens of children from Khambhatha and nearby settlements climb a narrow ladder fixed to a pillar of an unfinished bridge, edge past exposed steel bars, and cross above the fast-flowing water to reach primary, middle and high schools. A commute with no room for a misstep. Pairi is a seasonal, rain-fed river rising in Bhatigarh hills of Gariyaband.6 years on, incomplete bridge turns monsoon river crossing into daily gamble for childrenIn winter, it dwindles to a trickle. By summer, much of its bed dries into stretches of sand, allowing people to walk across or ride bicycles and bikes.But from mid-June through Sept, monsoon rain can swell the river, sending water surging across its bed and making the usual crossing perilous.The roughly 300m bridge between Deharguda and Khambhatha, about 5km from Mainpur tehsil headquarters, has been under construction for about six years.Despite complaints and official inspections, work crawls on. Residents said exposed iron bars have already injured people, while rain makes the ladder slick and rising water deepens the peril.The danger came into public view after residents recorded videos of children making the precarious crossing and shared them on social media.About a year ago, elected representatives and former collector inspected the bridge and directed officials and the contractor to speed up work.Villagers said they were assured it would be completed within about six months. That deadline has long since passed.Residents have warned of a road blockade on the national highway if the administration fails to act.Gariyaband collector Ranbir Sharma said he would visit the site. "I am speaking to officials and villagers to understand what immediate solution can be provided. We will review the project status, fix responsibility for any avoidable delay, and ensure that both a temporary safe passage and a time-bound plan for completion are worked out."The delay is starkest because Mainpur, bordering Odisha, was a Maoist stronghold for decades until sustained security operations in its deep forests ended their dominance last year, killing 24 insurgents between Jan and Sept - including top commanders Modem Balakrishna and Chalpati.As the area returns to normalcy, the bridge meant to make life easier has become a tightrope over a river.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Raipur | Silver Rate in Raipur | Bank Holidays in Raipur | Public Holidays in Raipur | Raipur AQI | Weather in Raipur | Petrol Price in Raipur | Diesel Price in Raipur | CNG Price in Raipur | LPG Price in RaipurStay updated with the latest Raipur news. articles.title: In 2010, Taiwan turned 1.5 million discarded PET bottles into Taipei’s EcoARK; the $4.22 million exhibition hall stood 26 metres high and resisted storms
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Taiwan opened a 26-metre-high exhibition hall in Taipei in 2010 whose walls were made from plastic bottles.The structure was called EcoARK, used about.
articles.body: Taiwan opened a 26-metre-high exhibition hall in Taipei in 2010 whose walls were made from plastic bottles.The structure was called EcoARK, used about 1.5 million recycled PET bottles and was designed to withstand storms, earthquakes and fire. The project was created by architect and structural engineer Arthur Huang and his company, Miniwiz, for the Taipei International Flora Exposition. Contemporary reports estimated the cost at about NT$133 million, or roughly $4.22 million at the time. The three-storey exhibition hall stretched about 130 metres and was built from interlocking blocks made from recycled plastic.The bottles became building blocksThe bottles were processed into a construction material called Polli-Brick, which is a lightweight, translucent block made from recycled polyethylene terephthalate, or PET. The resulting wall had a honeycomb-like structure. The individual blocks locked together, which created a rigid outer shell and left small spaces that helped bring daylight into the building.Far Eastern Group commissioned and developed the project with Miniwiz and other partners, and said the EcoARK team repeatedly tested the wall during construction because of safety concerns. The company said the structure could withstand wind, water, fire and earthquakes.The building was also designed with features that tried to reduce its energy demands. Rainwater was collected and used in an exterior water-cooling system, while the translucent walls admitted natural light into the exhibition spaces.More than 1.5 million bottles went into EcoARKTaipei's own records give the number as 1.52 million recycled PET bottles, and the city's account of the 2010 Flora Expo described EcoARK as the Pavilion of New Fashion. The building was part of the Yuanshan Park area and was an example of the exposition's emphasis on reducing waste and lowering energy consumption.Far Eastern said its recycling program gathered one million PET bottles in 2008 alone, with schools, families and other members of the public contributing bottles for the project. The bottles were processed into the Polli-Brick units used to construct the building's facade. Far Eastern later said the project used 600,000 hexagonal Polli-Bricks.The building was designed to survive Taipei's weatherArthur Huang said that the interlocking plastic containers were strong enough to block the elements and withstand storms or earthquakes, and the wall system was also light enough to make the structure easier to assemble and dismantle. That flexibility became part of the project's design, and its components could be taken apart and reused instead of treating the building as a conventional permanent structure.National Geographic later described EcoARK as a nine-storey exhibition building made from 1.5 million recycled plastic bottles, and the same report identified the structure as one of Huang's early projects in turning discarded materials into construction products. The difference between the contemporary description of a three-storey hall and National Geographic's later nine-storey description seems to come from how the unusually tall structure was characterized. The more consistent measurement across contemporary reports is its roughly 26-metre height.EcoARK did not remain at the expo foreverThe building's first major public role came with the Taipei International Flora Expo, which opened on November 6, 2010. EcoARK served as an exhibition pavilion during the event, which attracted millions of visitors.In June 2011, Taipei City Government reported that the Pavilion of New Fashion had been dismantled. Far Eastern said its PET blocks would be given new uses through an initiative that planned to place them at elementary schools damaged by Typhoon Morakot in 2009. The blocks could be incorporated into learning spaces, galleries, greenhouses, recycling areas and animal enclosures.The pavilion therefore had a relatively short life as a single building, and its materials were intended to have a longer one. The project later became one of the best-known examples that was associated with Huang's work in recycled construction materials. The 2010 pavilion was eventually gone, but the bottles that formed its walls were designed from the beginning to avoid having a single final destination.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Former Tropical Storm Edouard lingers over Texas, flooding homes and roads
articles.summary: Texas authorities rescued dozens of people from stranded cars, homes surrounded by floodwaters and an assisted living facility Wednesday as former Tropical Storm Edouard lingered over rural parts of the state.
articles.body: LIVINGSTON, Texas — Texas authorities rescued dozens of people from stranded cars, homes surrounded by floodwaters and an assisted living facility Wednesday as former Tropical Storm Edouard lingered over rural parts of the state and dumped nearly 2 feet of rain in some places. Heavy rains from the storm, which weakened into a tropical depression after making landfall Tuesday, were expected to threaten the eastern part of the state through Thursday morning, the National Weather Service said. Meanwhile, a burst of tropical weather persisted in the Pacific Ocean, where three hurricanes were churning in open waters. In Texas’ hard-hit Hardin County, about 85 miles (137 kilometers) northeast of Houston, officials said flooding, downed trees and powerlines, debris, and power outages were still creating hazardous conditions. Between 18 inches (45 centimeters) and 20 inches (51 centimeters) fell in parts of the county over the last two days, the weather service said. The average local monthly rainfall for September is just 5.51 inches (14 centimeters), said Nick Slaughter, a meteorologist with the weather service. Across the area close to the Louisiana border, schools and municipal offices were closed, and residents were told to stay home. Edouard downs trees, floods roads and leaves drivers stranded Hardin County’s office of emergency management said Wednesday afternoon that 12 motorists had to be rescued after driving into flooded roadways, two people had to be rescued from a flooded home, about 10 structures were damaged by trees and thousands were still without power. In Jefferson County, located about 80 miles (130 kilometers) northeast of Houston, the main concern was restoring power after trees and limbs were brought down during the storm, which had wind gusts up to 90 mph (144 kph), said Robert Grimm, the county emergency management coordinator. About 22,000 customers in the county were without power as of late Wednesday afternoon, nearly half of the 50,000 utility customers affected statewide, according to poweroutage.com. Grady Leger said that as the storm moved through Hardin County on Tuesday evening, a powerline went down by his home near Lumberton, and he could feel the vibration coming up from the ground. “Some blue and yellow, white sparks caught part of my dead tree on fire,” Leger said. An assisted living facility was damaged in Hardin County, and 21 people were evacuated, according to Texas Parks and Wildlife, whose game wardens assisted. Photos from the agency showed some officials wading in thigh-deep water in parts of the county. Edouard is expected to dissipate Thursday. 3 hurricanes are in the Pacific Ocean Hurricane Marie strengthened from a tropical storm on Wednesday well offshore of southwest Mexico in the Pacific, the Miami-based National Hurricane Center said. Swells generated by the storm were expected to affect parts of coastal southwestern Mexico and the Baja California peninsula over the next few days. They will likely spread to southern California over the weekend, the center said. Hurricane Lowell, a Category 4 storm, was hundreds of miles south of Hawaii on Wednesday. It briefly strengthened to a Category 5 storm before weakening again, and it was expected to remain powerful over the next several days. Swells generated by Lowell are likely to affect portions of the Hawaiian islands beginning Wednesday, the center said. Regarding Marie and Lowell, swells “are likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions,” the center said. Elsewhere in the Pacific, Hurricane Karina strengthened into a powerful Category 4 storm. Forecasters said it should weaken over the next few days.

articles.title: Cassandra Wilson, 2-time Grammy Award-winning jazz singer, dies at 70
articles.summary: Cassandra Wilson, the two-time Grammy Award-winning jazz singer, songwriter and producer has died.
articles.body: NEW YORK — Cassandra Wilson, the two-time Grammy Award-winning jazz singer, songwriter and producer has died. She was 70. Dubbed America’s best singer by Time magazine in 2001, Wilson was best known for her genre-bending voice, which expanded the boundaries of traditional blues-based jazz and worked effortlessly across folk, pop, R&B, country and beyond. At the heart of all her work was her idiosyncratic contralto, a soulful sound distinctly tied to her roots. As Jon Batiste put it in a eulogy on Wednesday, Wilson sounded like the South. She died in her native Jackson, Mississippi, on Tuesday morning, the Hinds County Coroner Jeramiah Howard confirmed. “It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of Cassandra Wilson, the Grammy Award-winning and legendary jazz artist. Cassandra Wilson transitioned peacefully at home, surrounded by family, close friends, and her manager,” said a statement from her manager to jazz radio station WBGO. From Jackson to the world Born and raised in Jackson to musician Herman B. Fowlkes and teacher Mary Fowlkes, Wilson showed an early love of music listening to Motown, Miles Davis and Thelonious Monk. At 6, she started piano lessons. She played clarinet in marching bands. She performed at coffeehouses and in cover bands while studying at Millsaps College and Jackson State University. In the early ‘80s, she mentored under jazz greats in New Orleans before moving to New York City and joining Steve Coleman’s M-Base Collective — eventually becoming its main vocalist. Her instantly recognizable voice earned her four Grammy nominations and two wins for best jazz vocal album. Those were in 1997 for “New Moon Daughter” and 2009 for “Loverly.” In 2015, it was Wilson who gave a special concert at the famed Apollo Theater to commemorate the 100th birthday of blues singer Billie Holiday, the legendary American jazz vocalist who died in New York City at age 44. That same year, Wilson released her last album, “Coming Forth by Day,” an homage to Holiday. In 2022, Wilson was named a National Endowment for the Arts Jazz Master, one of the highest honors awarded to jazz musicians in the United States. Tributes pour in “She had an unmistakable vocal tone, phrasing and her approach of weaving folkloric, R&B and diasporic music together with experimental and popular genres had a major impact on me,” Batiste said in his tribute to Wilson on Instagram. “Her Mississippi heritage was always present in everything no matter how expansive her artistry evolved,” he wrote in the caption of a clip showing them together on Brazilian TV in 2009. “She was one of the first people to take me on tour around the world, the great Cassandra Wilson.” Jackson Mayor John Horhn said the city “has lost an extraordinary native daughter, and the world has lost a singular musical voice.” “Cassandra Wilson carried the sound, spirit and history of Mississippi with her wherever her music reached,” said the mayor’s statement, shared with WJTV. “Her work had rare depth of character and a profound understanding of how music moves people, tells stories and connects generations.”

articles.title: Russia to close Goethe-Institut centres as Germany tensions escalate
articles.summary: Moscow to shut Goethe-Institut centres after Germany announces the closure of two Russian institutions.
articles.body:
Russia says it will close Germany’s Goethe-Institut cultural centres, Russian state media has reported, after Germany blamed Moscow for a drone incident at the Leipzig/Halle airport last month and said it would shutter a Russian cultural centre in Berlin and a consulate in Bonn.

Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said on Wednesday that Russia would close the centres in the cities of Moscow, Saint Petersburg and Yekaterinburg, following Germany’s decision to halt the operation of a Russian cultural centre in Berlin.

“They [Germany] deliberately took this step – they could not have failed to understand – which means the end of their cultural presence in Russia,” Lavrov said, according to state news agency TASS.

The Goethe-Institut cultural centres had stayed open “despite all the Ukrainian complications in our relations with the West,” he added.

The Kremlin said on Thursday that Germany was displaying an inconsistent and absurd position by choosing to shutter the Russian consulate in Bonn.

Last month’s incident involving an explosive-laden drone that started the chain of events has heightened fears over a sabotage campaign that the European Union and NATO say is a Russian attempt to destabilise Ukraine’s allies.

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt on Tuesday accused Russia of being behind the “hybrid attack”. The drone at Leipzig-Halle airport was found near a Ukrainian cargo plane on the evening of August 4 and defused.

On Tuesday, President Vladimir Putin accused Germany of planting evidence in order to blame Moscow for the drone incident.

“It is clear that it has all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said at a meeting of the bloc’s foreign ministers in Ireland.

“The question is, what do we do about this?”

Kallas said the EU had summoned the Russian envoy, and member states were doing the same.

“We will not let an act of such gravity go unpunished,” French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said, adding he had called in Russia’s envoy in Paris.

Kallas said that EU foreign ministers agreed to keep working on a proposal to impose sanctions on 1,600 individuals and entities linked to Russia’s military industry in the hope of adopting them next month.

“Seeing these hybrid attacks across Europe, I think these are also wake-up calls for the countries who have not been so strong … on this,” she said.

“If we want to end this war, we all have to focus our efforts. Take it to a new level.”

Russia’s first Goethe-Institut opened in Moscow in 1992, soon after the collapse of the Soviet Union. Following a diplomatic spat with Britain, Russia ordered the closure of its British Council in 2018.

On Wednesday, Lavrov’s deputy, Alexander Grushko, said Russia would retaliate “very soon” for the closure of the Bonn consulate.

articles.title: U.S. journalist sentenced to 2 years in federal prison for acting as an illegal agent for China
articles.summary: An American journalist has been sentenced to two years in federal prison for acting as an agent of a foreign government within the United States, the U.S.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — An American journalist has been sentenced to two years in federal prison for acting as an agent of a foreign government within the United States, the U.S. Justice Department said. Thomas Weir Pauken II, 51, pleaded guilty earlier this year and is not planning to appeal, according to his defense lawyer, Charles Burnham. Pauken also was sentenced to 36 months of supervised release with no overseas travel, the department said in a news release on Tuesday. He was arrested in February. The case is the latest in a series of federal prosecutions involving people accused of working for the Chinese government without proper disclosure, as tensions between Washington and Beijing remain high. “Pauken betrayed his country for money” for supporting “Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS) operations, recruiting, and gathering of sensitive information from potential assets,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg in the news release. Pauken worked as a journalist for various Chinese news organizations after moving to China in 2010, including state broadcaster CCTV. He most recently worked as an editor for Xinhua, China’s state news agency, a position he had held since 2024. “Mr. Pauken has accepted responsibility and respects the court’s sentence,” his lawyer said, adding that “as the government agreed in court, Mr. Pauken did not provide any classified information to the Chinese.” According to court documents, from at least 2019 until February 2026, Pauken worked at the direction of people he knew worked for China’s government, including a person he met in 2017 identified as “Cathy.” “Cathy” told him the reports were read by Chinese President Xi Jinping, according to a Feb. 27 federal court affidavit filed by FBI Special Agent Timothy J. Healy. Pauken received at least $100,000 for his work with “Cathy,” the department said. In addition to writing reports, Pauken was also asked by “Cathy” to recruit people to provide classified information. In one case, Pauken was instructed to meet with a person identified in the affidavit as “Person 1” and provide the person a Samsung phone, a computer, and passwords for Signal and Telegram, as well as NetDisk. Pauken was stopped by Customs and Border Protection agents when he returned to the U.S. in January 2025. In interviews with CBP and FBI agents, Pauken said he was “80 percent sure” that the person who was seeking a job in the Trump administration would provide classified information to China, although Pauken advised the person not to, according to the affidavit. Pauken also told investigators that “Cathy” would usually pay for his trips to the U.S. through the years, and often wired payments to his wife’s bank accounts, the affidavit said. China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs didn’t immediately respond on Wednesday to a request seeking comment. Pauken, a Texas native, used the alias of Tom McGregor when working as a commentator and writer at the request of his father, who shares his name and wanted to distance himself from his son’s work in China. The younger Pauken published two books under his real name, Thomas W. Pauken II. One was published in 2019 about U.S.-China relations and another in 2023 about Shenzhen, a city across from Hong Kong in mainland China. Pauken’s father was a former chairman of the Texas Republican Party in the 1990s and ran for governor more than a decade ago. In the most recent publicly visible Facebook post under McGregor’s name, Pauken shared photos of his wife and child on a trip, writing “My family and I enjoying our trip to Washington DC.” He was arrested later that month.

articles.title: Photos: Symbolic funerals held in Nepal for missing flood victims
articles.summary: Symbolic funerals held in Nepal for those still missing after deadly floods in the Himalayan nation.
articles.body:
Families in Nepal held symbolic funerals for relatives who remain missing, hoping to free their souls after they were presumed dead.

In Hindu tradition, cremation is a vital final rite, and for some families, performing the ceremony without the bodies of their loved ones has brought a measure of spiritual release.

Authorities in Nepal have meanwhile been burying recovered bodies in temporary graves until they can be identified. DNA samples are being preserved, distinguishing facial features photographed and other identifying details recorded to help match the remains with missing people and eventually return them to their families.

The August 26 flash flood has been one of the deadliest disasters to hit the Himalayan nation in recent years.

More than 1,200 people were killed and about 4,750 remain missing in Nepal and China’s Tibet region, after a huge wave of mud and debris destroyed towns, roads, bridges and several hydropower dams.

articles.title: Pessimists say the economy is weak. The good news is, they are wrong
articles.summary: Trump tax reforms sparked $296 billion in IRS refunds along with new deductions for qualified tips and overtime pay rewarding working Americans.
articles.body: The pessimists are wrong, and the numbers prove it. articles.title: Israeli flags and flattened homes: A rare look inside occupied southern Lebanon
articles.summary: Driving south along a coastal road in Israeli-occupied southern Lebanon, village after village lies in ruins, with homes systematically flattened by Israeli forces.
articles.body: Driving south on a coastal road in southern Lebanon, the Lebanese and Hezbollah flags that line the road suddenly switch to Israeli flags. Soon, an Israeli checkpoint comes into view, where soldiers stand watch from the balconies of homes riddled with shrapnel. And then, the landscape turns flat: Village after village, home after home, reduced to rubble. This is what Israeli-occupied Lebanon looks like. CNN gained rare access by joining a convoy of residents permitted to move through that occupied territory to reach their homes in three predominantly Christian villages. They have been spared the fate of the surrounding Shia Muslim villages that now resemble a wasteland. Israel invaded southern Lebanon in March after Hezbollah, a Shia Lebanese militant group backed by Iran, resumed strikes on Israel to avenge the assassination of Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Since then, the Israeli military has occupied a band of territory about 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) deep to establish what it calls a “security zone” to protect Israel’s northern residents from the threat of rocket attacks from Hezbollah. Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz vowed to destroy all homes in villages near the border. On the ground, the evidence of that is clear. Most villages have been systematically flattened by Israeli forces, and residents of the remaining Christian villages described hearing daily controlled demolitions in neighboring communities. According to the Lebanese Ministry of Health, more than 4,300 people have been killed by Israeli strikes since March 2, and the United Nations says more than 350,000 remain displaced since Israel’s occupation began. As our journey continues, the road twists through apocalyptic terrain until, out of nowhere, life reappears. Buildings stand intact, cars move through the streets and children ride their bikes, as life appears to go on as normal. But the reality is more complicated than appearances may suggest. The villages of Rmeish, Ain Ebel and Debel have been largely spared Israel’s bombardment and demolitions, but their residents – almost all of whom are Christian – are cut off from the rest of Lebanon, unable to go in or out without joining a UN-led convoy. Caritas, a Catholic non-profit that helps organize some of the convoys, must request permission for each resident from the Israeli military through a US-led monitoring mechanism. Approvals usually come, but the convoys are sometimes delayed or canceled, and the journey can take anywhere from a couple of hours to an entire day. Ronnie and Rita Alam fled Rmeish with their two daughters in March, as Israeli bombardment intensified around them. They rented a home in Beirut, which strained their finances. CNN met them as Ronnie drove his wife and daughters back to Rmeish for the first time in four months. Ronnie, however, must return to work in Beirut. “I’m happy that I’m returning to my home, but I’m unhappy because my husband won’t be with me,” Rita said, becoming emotional. “Our family is being separated,” she said, wiping off tears. “We are four, and now we will become three.” A ceasefire is technically in effect, but Israeli strikes continue in southern Lebanon on a daily basis. Israel insists this is allowed under the latest ceasefire agreement. Despite the risks, Ronnie said that financially there was no real alternative to sending his family back to their village. “Civilians have nothing to do with this. Why should they lose their homes? This destruction is a shame… and for what? For war? We don’t want war!” A besieged enclave Inside Ain Ebel, another of the majority Christian villages, Yorgos Mitri has gotten used to war. Even his 2-year-old son, Joe, can recognize the sound of fighter jets flying overhead, he said, and airstrikes no longer wake him at night. Surrounding Ain Ebel are the ruins of towns and villages hit by relentless Israeli bombardment, bulldozing and controlled demolitions. Mitri chose to stay through it all, out of attachment to his home and fear he might not be able to return to it. Like many Christians in these villages, he has no sympathy for Hezbollah, blaming the group for triggering the war that has turned the view from his home into a landscape of destruction. “You can see the results… what did we achieve after all of this?” he said, pointing to the ravaged town of Bint Jbeil. His anger at Hezbollah is matched by his sympathy for his civilian Shia Muslim neighbors, who have borne the brunt of Israel’s bombing and demolitions in the south. “Nobody deserves this,” he said, looking out at the devastated landscape. “We can’t live alone. We need to live all together.” He laments what he views as a weak and ineffective Lebanese government, which he says needs to regain control of its territory. Inside the ‘pilot zones’ For now, the Lebanese government is powerless to operate in the Israeli-occupied portion of the country. Under a US-led framework agreement between Israel and Lebanon signed in June, Israel is meant to hand over tiny pockets of the territory it occupies to the Lebanese army, establishing so-called “pilot zones.” But there is little indication the plan will go ahead as intended. It began in three villages, all Shia Muslim majority, but none had been fully occupied by Israeli forces to begin with – leading many to question whether Israel ever intended to withdraw. CNN exclusively joined the Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF) on a patrol mission to one of them, Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh. Lebanese soldiers deployed there are tasked with preventing armed non-state actors, like Hezbollah, from coming in; confiscating any weapons and remnants of war; and restoring state authority. The priority, according to Col. Raja Amer, the assistant to the commander of the South Litani sector, is making the area safe for displaced residents to return. But his forces face many challenges. The Lebanese economic crisis has gutted funding for the army. Soldiers earn an average of $500 a month, and much of their equipment is outdated or in short supply. “Our troops are operating in a very demanding and challenging security environment,” Amer told CNN. “This is why we need more capabilities to do these missions.” The risks include unexploded ordnance left behind by either Hezbollah or Israel and persistent Israeli airstrikes. According to the Lebanese army, 34 soldiers have been killed in 2026 alone. As a soldier spoke about a comrade he’d lost in a previous Israeli airstrike, Israel began shelling the nearby village of Mansouri – four strikes in less than 20 minutes. None of the soldiers reacted. For them, this was normal. Amer said the army had recorded more than 5,000 Israeli attacks on Lebanon since the framework agreement was signed in June. “It’s continuous and it’s everywhere… this is what the ‘ceasefire’ is from their side,” he said. In Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, there is no Israeli military presence. But just a couple of hundred yards away, Israeli tanks and bulldozers are visible, and the demolition of buildings continues apace. Soldiers and residents told CNN that drones fly overhead constantly, and they hear the sound of artillery shelling every day. It hardly feels like a ceasefire to those on the ground, nor do the pilot zones appear to be paving the way for Israel to withdraw from Lebanese territory. A history of sectarian strife Lebanon’s painful history of sectarian violence always simmers beneath the surface. For three years now, many have feared that Hezbollah’s war with Israel could be the spark that lights the tinderbox. Hezbollah draws much of its support from Shia Muslim-majority towns in southern Lebanon, which endured nearly two decades of Israeli occupation at the end of the last century, a situation compounded by a lack of economic opportunity and a sense of abandonment by the government in Beirut. Hezbollah, which is both a political party and militant group, came to be viewed by much of the Shia population as a protector against Israeli aggression and a provider of social services for a neglected community. The United States and United Kingdom have designated it as a terror group. On the drive CNN took with the Lebanese army, Hezbollah flags and posters commemorating fighters killed in the conflict lined most roads, a sign the group still enjoys significant support. “Hezbollah in Lebanon has a political part and a military part,” Amer said. “They are a part of this population. They were here, and the symbols stay in the place still now.” Israeli officials say the Lebanese army is not disarming Hezbollah fast enough by conducting more aggressive searches in people’s homes. However, Lebanese law bars the army from entering private property without a judicial warrant or legal authorization, which it currently does not have. Mindful of the country’s recent history of civil war, the Lebanese military says it is taking care to avoid fueling sectarian strife. “Doing things in violence against our own people, it will be also with other consequences,” Amer said. “We will do this slowly. We will do this in a reasonable way.” Negotiations between Israel and Lebanon have stalled, with no sign Israel intends to withdraw its forces from occupied territory. Israel’s Defense Minister has said the military would not withdraw from Lebanon even if the United States demanded it. With Israeli elections set for October, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will likely want to hand his base a clear victory on this front. Amer said the Lebanese army was prepared to take on more pilot zones if political negotiations bear fruit but warned the effort won’t succeed if conditions mirror the first attempt. “We stuck to the agreement. We need the other part to stick to the agreement too and to cease fire, at the very least,” he said. Fewer than one in 20 of Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh’s residents have returned home so far, according to the Lebanese army – a figure it hopes to see rise. Mahmoud Darwish is one of them, having come back after the army deployed to the village. Speaking with CNN, he didn’t explicitly voice support for Hezbollah but said anyone attacked has the right to resist with force. Darwish was displaced for five months. When he returned in July, he found his home badly damaged – rubble up to his knees, soot darkening the walls. He said the village lived off farming, and that the now destroyed olive trees in his garden had long been his livelihood. Walking through the rubble, he placed one palm flat against a wall, then held it up – blackened. “This is Israel and America,” he said, raising it up. “And this is Lebanon, us,” he said, raising his clean hand. “They killed us, they killed our people, killed our loved ones, killed our friends, destroyed our homes. How do they think they’ll ever make peace with us?” As he spoke, an Israeli airstrike thudded in the distance. Darwish barely flinched. “No enemy will ever remove us from our land … she loves me and I love her … we are here and we will remain here.”

articles.title: The cure for socialism is giving more Americans a stake in capitalism
articles.summary: Socialism is gaining ground because fewer Americans are homeowners and stockholders, creating a perfect opening for DSA leaders like Zohran Mamdani.
articles.body: With each passing election, the socialist surge is rising. Bernie Sanders-backed Abdul El-Sayed won the Michigan Democratic Senate primary, defeating a well-funded establishment candidate. In Wisconsin, Francesca Hong — a democratic socialist who once called for canceling Thanksgiving — came within 3,000 votes of winning her state's gubernatorial primary. The DSA darling Zohran Mamdani is already the mayor of America’s largest city. Some argue that socialism has hit its high-water mark and is losing momentum. Count me skeptical. Socialism is gaining ground because, for too many, capitalism has become a spectator sport. The biggest reason more voters support state ownership is that fewer people are owners themselves. Consider the numbers. The national homeownership rate sits at 65% — down from a peak of 69.2% in 2004 and below the 25-year average. Among Americans under 35, it has fallen to just 35.2%, down more than a percentage point from a year ago. The generational gap is stark: Just 57% of Americans in their mid-30s own homes today compared to 64% of their parents' generation at the same age. With the 30-year mortgage rate recently climbing 6.69%, the homeownership rate is not about to improve anytime soon. BILLIONS SPENT BY KEY FEDERAL AGENCY HASN'T MADE AMERICAN DREAM OF HOMEOWNERSHIP ANY EASIER: REPORT The picture is similar in financial markets. Sixty-two percent of Americans own stock — but that number conceals the real story. Only 28% of households earning under $50,000 own any stock at all; for those with only a high school education or less, it's 42%, and for those 18 to 29, it’s 44%. Declining ownership rates create a perfect opportunity for the far left. People with property don’t like the government taking it. People without ownership see government-sponsored theft as more acceptable. Because it’s not state ownership that invigorates voters, but the promise that they too can share in the wealth of society. THE NUMBERS DON’T LIE. YOUNG AMERICANS ARE FALLING IN LOVE … WITH SOCIALISM This puts into perspective policies like Mamdani’s rent freeze — a false antidote to the difficulty of owning a home in New York. Rent freezes promise that people can stay in their apartments and the market cannot move them out. Likewise, when Sanders touts legislation to give the government a 50% stake in AI companies, it makes people feel like they have a stake in America’s biggest companies even if they don’t actually own a single stock. Yet these policies attempt to address symptoms while worsening the disease. A rent freeze may let you stay in an apartment owned by somebody else, but it proactively prevents actual ownership by reducing supply, degrading building quality and making conditions worse. And a government stake in AI companies may well flood the coffers of the IRS. But that does nothing to give actual people a stake in the success of high-growth companies. EL-SAYED REVEALS HE WOULD GO ‘STEP FURTHER’ THAN SANDERS ON SOCIALIST PLAN FOR MAJOR US INDUSTRY Still, however true these arguments are, they aren’t persuading voters. The most effective answer to Mamdani and the Democratic Socialists of America is not to point out the problems with socialism — it’s to give people an actual stake in society by increasing the number of homeowners and shareholders who have an interest in America’s success. Founders and employees with skin in the game think longer term. They protect customers, watch costs, solve problems and weather downturns differently because the outcome is partly theirs. They certainly don’t appreciate heavy-handed government. And while not everyone is called to be a business owner, nearly everyone can be a homeowner. Business coalitions should be pushing cities to permit more housing, shorten approval times and clear the regulatory barriers that make construction expensive. Companies can complement those efforts with matched savings programs, closing-cost assistance and financial coaching for first-time buyers. As AI threatens corporate headcounts, empowers small business development and accelerates the pandemic-induced emptying of downtown office buildings, we can also convert surplus commercial space into residential units. Adaptive reuse avoids the embodied carbon of demolition and new construction — and buildings account for nearly 37% of total U.S. energy consumption. Bringing underutilized commercial space back to productive residential use is one of the most practical emissions reductions available in the built environment, delivering a housing win and a climate win simultaneously. AMERICA’S BROKEN PERMITTING SYSTEM IS QUIETLY RAISING YOUR COST OF LIVING The path to stock ownership needs to be widened too. Broad-based equity compensation — stock grants, profit-sharing, employee stock ownership plans — can turn workers into partners in growth. Automatic retirement enrollment, meaningful employer matching and access to low-cost diversified investments can give workers a stake in American prosperity even before they can afford a home, especially if those investments are tied to high-growth fields like artificial intelligence or clean energy. None of this requires turning companies into charities. It is capitalism with aligned incentives — workers who accumulate assets, communities that keep their employers and a free-enterprise system defended by people protecting something they actually own. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The DSA sells government control because too many Americans believe the private economy has no place for them. The strongest defense of capitalism is opening a credible path for people to not only find their place, but to own it.

articles.title: Gulf insecurity fuels US energy dominance
articles.summary: The no-war, no-peace status quo with Iran increasingly benefits the US, its energy sector and its ally Israel.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump celebrated on Truth Social what he called the “biggest oil deal in history” – a 100-year concession on 17 oil fields in Venezuela that would secure 65 billion barrels of oil.

Around the same time, QatarEnergy informed Edison, one of its biggest European customers, that force majeure on its liquefied natural gas (LNG) deliveries would continue until early November. Five more cargoes were cancelled, taking the total to 29, or about 3.8 billion cubic metres of gas.

The contract has run since 2009 and normally covers roughly a tenth of Italy’s annual consumption. Edison has kept supplying its customers by finding replacement cargoes elsewhere, including in the US.

For decades, the bargain between Washington and the Gulf was clear. The US protected the region and kept its sea lanes open; Gulf producers supplied the energy on which the global economy depended and settled their sales in dollars to benefit the US economy.

That bargain has been turned on its head. America no longer simply protects Gulf energy. It competes with it, and increasingly profits when the Gulf cannot deliver due to insecurity.

Six months of war have reportedly impacted Qatar’s LNG exports significantly. Other Gulf countries like Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the UAE have seen a substantial drop in oil exports as well. Meanwhile, US oil and gas have moved into the space left behind, with US energy giants raking in record-high profits.

It is important here to distinguish between the US as a government and the dense network of private interests that operates around it. Washington wants strategic leverage over Iran and continued influence over the Gulf states. Energy companies want access to reserves, favourable regulation, profitable prices and new customers. Trump brings the two together under the banner of energy dominance. State power opens the door; private capital walks through it.

Israel adds another layer. Chevron operates its two main offshore gas fields, owning almost 40 percent of the Leviathan gasfield and 25 percent of the Tamar gasfield. Leviathan is expanding after a $35bn agreement was signed last year to increase exports to Egypt.

Israel is therefore not an independent energy rival to the US in the way Qatar is. Its growing role as an Eastern Mediterranean gas hub is tied to a US operator and fits comfortably within a US-backed regional system linking Israel, Egypt and Jordan.

Chevron is the thread running through much of this story. It has major interests in US production, controls Israel’s most important gas assets and is positioned to expand in Venezuela. This does not mean Chevron determines foreign policy. It does show how easily the exercise of American power can translate into commercial opportunity for American companies.

Israel is also determined not to let the confrontation with Iran end on terms it considers not to be in its interest. The US-Iran memorandum of understanding signed in June fell well short of Israeli war aims. Israel said it was not bound by all its provisions, insisted on freedom of action in Lebanon and briefly resumed attacks while the US was trying to sustain negotiations.

For Israel, ceasefires have tended to be pauses, not settlements: opportunities to regroup while preserving the option of striking again. The reasons are chiefly strategic. Israel wants to prevent Iran from rebuilding its nuclear, missile and regional capabilities, while Israeli leaders fear accepting a deal and looking weak ahead of elections.

The consequences of Israel pushing for continuous conflict align with US energy interests. Continued pressure on Iran keeps the Strait of Hormuz insecure, Gulf exports vulnerable and risk premiums for energy transport high. Israel and US energy companies do not need to be following a common plan for their interests to reinforce one another.

Price is where the argument becomes clearest. Trump talks constantly about cheap oil, but US producers cannot prosper if it becomes too cheap. A Dallas Federal Reserve survey found that US companies needed an average price of about $43 a barrel to operate existing wells and $66 to drill new ones profitably. The two main Permian basins sit at roughly $61 to $62.

Trump therefore needs a narrow band: oil cheap enough to contain inflation, but expensive enough to keep shale, fracking and export investment alive. Gulf insecurity helps maintain it. The disruption need not be catastrophic. It only has to keep prices at a point where the next American well makes economic sense.

This may help explain the attraction of a no-war, no-peace outcome. A full regional war could close Hormuz, send prices soaring and threaten Chevron’s Israeli operations. A durable settlement would remove the risk premium, restore confidence in Gulf supply and limit Israel’s freedom of action.

Managed insecurity sits conveniently between the two: enough restraint to protect US-linked production, but not enough diplomacy to make Gulf energy entirely dependable again.

Israel keeps Iran under pressure. Washington retains leverage over its allies. US producers gain customers and commercially supportive prices. The danger lies in the convergence: Several powerful actors now have something to gain from preventing the crisis from reaching a final resolution.

The Gulf still holds vast reserves and enjoys production costs US companies cannot match. But reserves alone no longer decide market power. Reliability does. Only an estimated 3.5 to 5.5 million barrels a day can bypass Hormuz through Saudi and Emirati pipelines. The rest remains exposed to a single point of failure, despite decades of arms purchases, foreign bases and security guarantees.

The greatest threat to the Gulf’s energy future is not depletion. It is that customers learn to live without it. Every delayed tanker strengthens the case for an Atlantic alternative. Every Qatari cargo replaced by US LNG creates a relationship that may endure long after the war.

US power once rested partly on protecting the flow of Gulf energy. It now rests increasingly on replacing it.
