articles.title: Magnitude 5 quake hits Tibet amid ongoing search for hundreds missing after deadly floods
articles.summary: China News: An earthquake of magnitude 5 struck Tibet on Thursday, according to the German Research Centre for Geosciences (GFZ).The quake occurred at a depth of .
articles.body: An earthquake of magnitude 5 struck Tibet on Thursday, according to the German Research Centre for Geosciences (GFZ).The quake occurred at a depth of 10 km (6.21 miles), GFZ said.The earthquake struck as rescue and recovery operations continued in Tibet following catastrophic flooding near the Gyirong border crossing with Nepal last week.China on Wednesday fully reopened the only road leading to the Gyirong crossing after sections of it were washed away, allowing heavy machinery to reach the main disaster zone for the first time, Reuters reported.The damage to the G216 national highway had earlier forced authorities to airdrop equipment and supplies to frontline rescuers, while some teams trekked through the mountains to reach the affected area.China's official death toll from the flooding in Tibet had risen to 21 by Wednesday, with 541 people still missing, according to Reuters.The missing included 104 Nepali citizens, 49 Indians, 33 Latvians and six Canadians, authorities had previously said.Rescue operations have been hampered by persistent rain, unstable cliffs and the fast-flowing river in the narrow mountain gorge, though authorities said the risks from monitored upstream lakes had diminished. Landslides, however, remained a concern.Nepal flood toll rises to 1,252; over 4,200 still missingAcross the border, Nepal's flash flood death toll has risen to 1,252, while around 4,216 people remain missing or out of contact, according to the latest update issued by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) on Thursday.The highest number of bodies has been recovered from Chitwan, at 355, followed by Nawalparasi East with 218, Nawalparasi West with 208, Nuwakot with 177 and Rasuwa with 127. Bodies have also been recovered from Gorkha, Dhading and Tanahun.Only 95 bodies have so far been identified and handed over to relatives, according to the NDRRMA.Around 11,993 people have been rescued and 5,135 injured people have received medical treatment. The missing include about 900 people linked to hydroelectric projects, as well as around 583 foreign citizens and 164 Nepalis accompanying foreign tourists.Search and rescue operations remain focused on areas affected by landslides, floodwaters and debris, with more than 21,000 security personnel deployed for rescue, search and relief operations.Rescue efforts have increasingly centred on hydropower tunnels, where authorities believe some of the missing workers may have survived after being cut off by floodwaters and debris, Reuters reported.“We are very confident that there is life in there because ... there is food and water in the building, that was likely built for communication purposes and as a resting place,” Amshu Kiran Shahi, a board member of the Nepal Electricity Authority, told Reuters.Nepal foreign minister Shisir Khanal, meanwhile, described the disaster as a “Himalayan Tsunami” while briefing diplomats in Kathmandu on Thursday.“I want to call the disaster the Himalayan Tsunami as we have not experienced such a massive disaster in our recent memory,” Khanal said.The flash floods, triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, devastated towns and villages across northern and central Nepal.Specialised rescue teams from India, China and the United States were involved in tunnel rescue attempts.Meanwhile, Nepal plans to rebuild an early-warning system for landslides along part of its border with China after the glacial flood swept away existing monitoring infrastructure, Reuters reported, citing two Nepali government sources.The new system is expected to include seismic sensors, cameras and a satellite link to help authorities monitor fresh hazards and issue warnings.The immediate danger from two barrier lakes near the border has passed after they drained, but the terrain remains unstable and is being closely watched.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Carla Jeffery: 'Beautiful, vibrant' Disney star dies at 33
articles.summary: Jeffery was known for playing cheerleader Bree in 2018 Disney Channel movie Zombies and two sequels.
articles.body:
US actress Carla Jeffery, who was known for appearing in 2018 Disney Channel movie Zombies and two sequels, has died at the age of 33.

Announcing the news, her agent Carla Alexander described her as a "beautiful, vibrant and incredibly talented woman whose radiant smile could light up any room".

Jeffery played cheerleader Bree in Zombies and its follow-ups in 2020 and 2022, and previously had a recurring role in Curb Your Enthusiasm as one of the Black family, who moved in with Larry David after Hurricane Katrina.

Her management company Alexanders Talent wrote on Instagram : "Our hearts are broken as we mourn the loss of our beloved Carla Jeffery.

"For more than 20 years, Carla was part of the Alexanders Talent Management family and watching her grow from a talented young girl into the beautiful, vibrant woman and actress she became was an incredible privilege.

"We will remember her infectious smile, her laughter, her talent, and the beautiful light she carried everywhere she went.

"Our deepest love and condolences are with Carla's family and loved ones. We ask that their privacy be respected during this incredibly difficult time. Rest beautifully, Carla. You will be deeply missed and forever loved."

Jeffery's twin brother Carlon, who is also an actor, reposted that statement as well as a clip of his sister on a beach and a screenshot of an undated text message.

"Hey Sis, call me back when you get this. I was just calling to see how your day went! I love you to the moon & back sis," it read.

"I just want you to know how proud I am of you. Your resilience, your grace, your infectious smile that lights up a room. You are truly a light that shines bright. Don't let anyone dim that light, even yourself.

"The light you carry is special and must be protected at all times. You are the best sister a brother could ask for. Pray we continue to grow closer to one another along this journey. I got your back in this life and the next."

Her co-stars also paid tribute, with Chandler Kinney, who played Willa in Zombies, writing that the actress's death "doesn't feel real".

"Carla. The sweetest, most sparkly gal. You made every day better and brighter with your infectious positivity," Kinney wrote.

"I think part of why you brought such effervescence to Bree (aside from your immense talent) is because that's really who you were in your heart; a bubbly, vivacious heart-of-gold cheerleader who loved nothing more than to uplift those around her."

Milo Manheim, who played Zed, shared a series of photos with the caption: "Love you Carlaboo, the sweetest, kindest, most loving person."

articles.title: Rescue efforts continue as Nepal-China flood death toll surpasses 1,270
articles.summary: Authorities in Nepal use helicopters and zip lines to reach remote flood-stricken villages amid widespread destruction.
articles.body:
Rescue teams in Nepal are working around the clock to reach workers trapped inside hydropower facilities more than a week after flash floods devastated entire communities in the Himalayas.

Last week, a cascade of rocks, mud and water that scientists believe came from a glacier collapse near the Langtang Lirung mountain peak swept away villages, roads, and bridges in Nepal and Tibet.

More than 1,270 people have been killed, and more than 4,700 are still missing, authorities said on Thursday.

Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said 1,252 bodies have been recovered as the total number of missing in the country remained at 4,216. Hundreds of workers are believed to be trapped inside hydropower plants, including some in tunnels, near the country’s border with China.

In neighbouring Tibet, Chinese authorities have reported 21 deaths and 541 people missing.

“We still hope there are some survivors inside,” Sanjay Kc, an officer from the Nepalese army engineering department, said, in front of bulldozers trying to remove huge piles of mud blocking the entrance of a tunnel in the Rasuwa district, one of the worst affected areas in Nepal. “Because it’s a big power house inside, so it’s a big room, and we feel that the whole power house is not flooded,” he told Al Jazeera.

Families of those missing are gathering each morning hoping for news about their loved ones. For many, the wait is excruciating.

“Every day I come here hoping to find my father,” said Pratik Rana, the son of a missing engineer. “But every day at sunset I feel my hope fades away… [A] father is equally important for everyone, but for me he was a precious part of my life.”

In other affected areas, authorities are using all available tools, including zip lines and helicopters, to rescue people trapped in remote villages. The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) estimated floods and mudflows have left at least 2.2 million tonnes of debris.

In the capital Kathmandu, forensic teams are working to identify bodies.

Al Jazeera’s Jessica Washington, reporting from a DNA testing facility in the city, said many of the bodies being found are in a state of decomposition.

“Forensic teams on the ground told us that there are some things that can help with the identification process, such as tattoos and jewellery, but many bodies were found in such a state that it’s very challenging to identify them.”

On Wednesday, the country’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah said authorities would continue searching for survivors while also starting rehabilitation and rebuilding efforts.

Dharma Raj Upreti, chief of the NDRRMA, told the Reuters news agency that about 20,000 houses would have to be rebuilt, including 7,500 that have been destroyed.

“There is no point in rebuilding the houses in the same locations, as that would expose people to the same risks,” Upreti told the news agency, adding that authorities were trying to identify safer areas to relocate the communities and build up new settlements. As of Monday, the UN said more than 3,400 displaced people were living in 27 displacement sites in Nuwakot and Rasuwa, mostly in schools.

Nepali authorities have pointed to the role of major greenhouse gas emitters that have a “historical responsibility to compensate vulnerable nations like Nepal”, said Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal. He added that the government has officially filed a “formal climate compensation claim letter” to international partners.

images.caption: People look at photographs of missing people on a wall outside Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital following the deadly flash floods and mudslides, in Kathmandu, Nepal [Athit Perawongmetha/Reuters]

articles.title: Spain’s PM says he received no advance warnings of Ceuta influx as he defends handling of crisis
articles.summary: Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has denied accusations that the government ignored warnings about an impending mass border crossing from Morocco to the enclave of Ceuta.
articles.body: Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has denied accusations that the government ignored warnings about an impending mass border crossing from Morocco to the enclave of Ceuta. Sánchez has been under intense pressure over the crisis, which saw an estimated 72,000 people cross the border. Dozens died and many remain in the city. In an address to parliament on Thursday, Sánchez said that there had been no “alerts or special notices” prior to July 30-31. “We have examined all of the messages, statements and verbal reports from the state security apparatus,” he said. “I can assure you that none of them went any further than a description of the data or routine reporting, and that absolutely none of them predicted the probability or the scale of what ended up occurring.” Defending his government’s handling of the crisis, Sánchez promised to publish a dossier of official reports showing all of the information that was available to the government. “The government has nothing to hide on this matter,” he said. Although most of the migrants have since crossed back over the border to Morocco, the incident has become a significant political issue for Sánchez and his government both at home and abroad. Tens of thousands of people took to the streets of Ceuta and other cities around Spain on Wednesday in protest against the government. Relations with Morocco have been strained following reports that its government had facilitated the mass border crossing, but Sánchez tamped down the speculation. “Lots of people think that the Moroccan authorities provoked this crisis,” he said. “Up to this point, no one has provided any definitive proof to the government that would allow us to conclude that this mass border crossing… was planned or executed by the Moroccan authorities,” he said, adding that investigations were ongoing as to whether they had in fact played any role in the incident. Sánchez added that the two countries would continue to cooperate on border issues, but “it’s clear that after what happened this cooperation has to be different.” The incident has also caused diplomatic issues within the European Union (EU), with anti-immigration leaders such as Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni calling for Spain’s membership of the Schengen visa-free travel area to be suspended. Italy also temporarily toughened controls on travel from the country. The spat became so hostile that Jose Manuel Albares, Spain’s foreign minister, summoned the Italian ambassador on July 31 to discuss comments made by his Italian counterpart Antonio Tajani, who claimed, without evidence, that Madrid’s immigration policy “encourages human trafficking.” At the time, Sánchez pointed out that Ceuta is not part of the Schengen area, singled out Italy as a country that lets in more illegal migrants than Spain, and accused other European states of providing “very little support” to Madrid. On Thursday, Sánchez said that he would ask for support from EU institutions such as Frontex, the bloc’s border and coastguard agency, in securing borders at both Ceuta and Melilla, Spain’s other enclave on the North African coast. Both are claimed by Morocco. “We are going to ask that a permanent Frontex presence be established,” he said, as well as requesting a special Europol mission to monitor irregular migration to Ceuta. The Spanish government will also ask the EU to recognize Ceuta and Melilla as outermost regions of the bloc, a special designation that allows territories that are separate from mainland Europe to join the EU customs union, said Sánchez. An estimated 10,000 migrants remain in Ceuta, which has a permanent population of around 80,000 people, causing social tensions in the enclave and providing a talking point for Spain’s insurgent far-right. However Sánchez also acknowledged that it is impossible to completely prevent border crossings. “We aren’t going to guarantee that these borders are 100% secure, because behind them lie inequality and a search for opportunity, and no matter how high that border (wall) is, this is always going to be the case,” he said.

articles.title: Palestinian teens killed during settler attack on West Bank village, officials say
articles.summary: Al-Mughayyir's council says they were trying to stop settlers stealing sheep, but the Israeli military says they threw stones at its troops.
articles.body:
Funerals have taken place for two Palestinian teenagers who local officials say were killed by Israeli settlers and soldiers in an attack on their village in the occupied West Bank on Wednesday.

The village council in al-Mughayyir told the BBC that Omar al-Nassan, 19, and Khalil Abu Alia, 16, were killed as they tried to stop Israeli settlers stealing sheep and that confrontations broke out.

The Israeli military stated that its forces had entered the village to provide security for an Israeli civilian and police trying to retrieve livestock.

It said they fired on and struck what it called "key instigators" of a "violent disturbance", in which Palestinians threw stones at its troops.

The deaths come amid a recent surge in settler violence in the West Bank, with more than three attacks per day on average recorded by the UN so far this year.

Al-Mughayyir, near Ramallah, has seen repeated settler attacks.

At least 81 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank since the start of the year, according to the UN's figures. At least 23 of those deaths have occurred in the context of settler attacks.

Three Israelis, both security forces and civilians, have been killed by Palestinians in the West Bank over the same period, the UN says.

The Israeli military has faced mounting criticism for actively participating in settler attacks on Palestinians, standing by, or failing to prosecute those responsible.

On Thursday, Israel's police force said a 19-year-old settler had been arrested on suspicion of participating in an attack on the Palestinian village of Qusra on Saturday. It marks the first such arrest in weeks of attacks on Qusra.

Dozens of masked settlers descended on the village, surrounding a house while Palestinians were trapped inside, and throwing stones.

Israeli soldiers who were deployed to the scene reportedly detained the trapped Palestinians but not the settlers, allowing them to leave. The Israeli military said troops removed "rioters" and protected residents.

Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem - land Palestinians want, along with Gaza, for a future state - during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.

The settlements are illegal under international law.

In a separate development on Wednesday, Israeli forces demolished the Palestinian village of Khirbet al-Tabban, in the Masafer Yatta area.

Israeli human rights group B'Tselem said the village's 70 residents, including 28 children, were given no warning prior to the demolition and were not allowed to remove their property.

It described the demolition as the most significant in Masafer Yatta since May 2025.

In the 1980s, the Israeli military declared about 3,000 hectares in the South Hebron Hills, which includes Masafer Yatta, as a restricted firing zone for training purposes.

The military says the Palestinian homes there have been built illegally.

In 2022, Israel's Supreme Court ruled to allow the demolition of homes in the firing zone and the expulsion of their residents, who had argued that such a move violated international law and that their families had been living there since before the State of Israel was established.

B'Tselem says Khirbet al-Tabban is the 66th Palestinian community to be expelled by Israeli authorities since the start of the Gaza war in October 2023, which it alleges is part of a campaign of "ethnic cleansing" being carried out in the West Bank.

articles.title: DHS directs ICE attorneys to seek early dismissal of legally deficient asylum claims
articles.summary: DHS is directing ICE attorneys to seek early dismissal of asylum claims deemed legally insufficient, allowing judges to decide them without a full merits hearing.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE – The Department of Homeland Security has issued new guidance directing its immigration attorneys to seek early dismissal of asylum claims they determine are legally insufficient, according to internal guidance obtained by Fox News Digital. Effective immediately, attorneys with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's (ICE) Office of the Principal Legal Advisor (OPLA) are expected to seek dismissal of asylum applications they determine fail to meet the legal standard on their face by filing motions to pretermit in immigration court. A motion to pretermit asks an immigration judge to deny an asylum application before a full merits hearing because the government argues the application is legally insufficient. Immigration judges ultimately decide whether to grant those motions. ICE SEEKS NEARLY $500K FINE AGAINST IMMIGRATION LAWYER ACCUSED OF FILING FAKE ASYLUM CLAIMS The guidance is intended to expedite the adjudication of asylum claims that satisfy the legal requirements while allowing the government to challenge deficient applications earlier in the immigration court process. The directive also reinforces the administration's ongoing focus on combating asylum fraud, including continued efforts to hold attorneys accountable for facilitating fraudulent asylum claims. TRUMP ADMIN EYES HISTORIC MASS VISA REVOCATION TARGETING UP TO 200K ASYLUM SEEKERS: REPORT The policy follows a series of recent administration actions aimed at reshaping the asylum system. Earlier this year, the administration streamlined portions of the affirmative asylum process by allowing certain applications to move directly to immigration court without first undergoing asylum interviews, a change officials said would reduce duplicative reviews and help address the immigration court backlog. The administration has also expanded its focus on asylum fraud. In recent months, ICE announced a policy allowing the agency to pursue civil penalties against attorneys accused of facilitating fraudulent asylum claims and later sought financial penalties against a New York immigration attorney accused of filing fraudulent asylum applications. TRUMP SCORES SCOTUS ASYLUM WIN — BUT LIBERAL JUSTICE WARNS IT COULD BACKFIRE AT BORDER The latest guidance extends that broader effort into immigration court litigation by directing government attorneys to challenge asylum claims they believe do not satisfy the legal requirements before those cases proceed to full evidentiary hearings. articles.title: Why restaurant servers clear your plate before everyone finishes eating
articles.summary: An etiquette experts reveal the subtle body language cues that restaurant servers use to decide when to clear your plate and what diners often get wrong.
articles.body: Your empty dinner plate may be disappearing faster than etiquette says it should. Traditional dining etiquette calls for restaurants to wait until everyone at a table has finished eating before clearing the plate. But many contemporary restaurants clear plates individually, creating an awkward question for diners: Is the server simply being attentive or are you being hurried out? "Everyone at the table should be finished before all the plates are cleared," Jacqueline Whitmore, Florida-based founder of the Protocol School of Palm Beach, told Fox News Digital. FED UP WITH SCREAMING KIDS AT DINNER? MORE AMERICANS SUPPORT ADULTS-ONLY DINING Salar Sheik, who runs Savory Hospitality Restaurant Consulting in Los Angeles, said diners shouldn't automatically interpret a cleared plate as a hint to leave. "Clearing a plate is not necessarily an attempt to rush the guest or turn the table," Sheik told Fox News Digital. "Often, the server is simply trying to keep the table tidy, maintain the flow of service and prepare for the next course." Knowing exactly when to clear a plate, however, requires some finesse. Sheik said servers may look for cues such as a diner pushing a plate away, putting silverware together, sitting back from the table or looking around for the server when little or no food remains. "We train the best service professionals to read the guest's body language, pace and overall energy to determine when it is appropriate to approach and clear a plate," Sheik said. "This is a subtle skill that only a small percentage of staff members truly master." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Getting it wrong can have exactly the effect diners suspect. Repeatedly hovering or trying to remove a plate while someone is still eating "can make the guest feel rushed and is a sign of poor service," Sheik said. There are ways diners can signal whether they're finished, Whitmore said. Crossing a knife and fork on the plate indicates that a customer is still eating or resting, the etiquette expert said. Placing the utensils side by side at roughly the four-o'clock position indicates the meal is finished. Sheik also points to silverware as a cue, though he cautions that such signals aren't completely universal. Customs can vary among countries and restaurants, he said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The simplest solution may be to skip the guesswork altogether. "If there is any doubt, the server should always ask, 'May I clear this for you?'" Sheik said. While restaurants shouldn't make customers feel rushed, diners have responsibilities, too. There is no universal limit on how long a party should occupy a table, Sheik said. It depends on factors including the restaurant, size of the party, waiting reservations and whether a specific dining time has been communicated, he said. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Whitmore's advice is similarly situational: "Read the room." If diners are lingering while a line of customers waits for a table, they should be mindful of those around them. If no one is waiting, she said, they should "go ahead and enjoy" themselves. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Ultimately, good service may depend less on decoding a diner's body language than on five simple words: "May I clear this for you?"

articles.title: Built in the 1880s with 48 rooms, a Louisville mansion later helped inspire the Speed Art Museum; nearly 140 years later, it is for sale for $1.95 million
articles.summary: News News: A Louisville landmark is back on the market, giving potential buyers a chance to own a sprawling mansion tied to one of the city's most important cult.
articles.body: A Louisville landmark is back on the market, giving potential buyers a chance to own a sprawling mansion tied to one of the city's most important cultural institutions. The Speed Mansion, a 48-room home at 505 W. Ormsby Ave. in Old Louisville, sports a $1.95 million listing price, states an online report by WDRB + WAVE website. The three-story property has been used primarily as office and educational space in recent years, but its next chapter could be very different, adds the news report. The mansion, built in the 1880s, was originally owned by Louisville homebuilder Dexter Belknap, Some eight years after its construction, businessman, philanthropist and art collector James Breckinridge J.B. Speed bought the property. peed and his wife, Hattie Bishop Speed, would leave a legacy linking the home to Louisville’s arts community. Hattie Bishop Speed was a concert pianist and music instructor. After her husband’s death she remained at the mansion, adding a recital hall to the back of the property in 1916. The addition reflected the wider artistic interests of the couple, and helped to turn the mansion into a center of cultural and educational activity.A legacy that lives outside the MansionThe strongest link to the property occurred in 1925 when Hattie Bishop Speed founded the J.B. Speed Memorial Museum in memory of her husband. The institution eventually became the one of Louisville’s best-known cultural institutions. What began as a memorial to J.B. Speed has become a major art museum, with a collection and public presence far exceeding the original mansion. The Speed Mansion itself changed through the years. More recently, it was used by the Kentucky College of Art + Design as an office and educational space. The college has since relocated to a larger campus on Garvin Place in Old Louisville, making the historic property available for a new owner.New possibilities for a historic houseThe mansion's next incarnation could be far removed from its recent life. The listing agent said in the WDRB + WAVE exclusive report that the property could be redeveloped into apartments or converted into a boutique hotel, giving developers a chance to re-purpose the historic building, while maintaining its ties to Louisville’s past. There is plenty of scope for possibilities with 48 rooms and three stories, but any redevelopment would have to take the historic nature of the property into account.Back on the marketThe mansion last sold in 2018 for $1.5 million, according to public records in Jefferson County, Louisville Business First reports. The home, now listed at $1.95 million, is again drawing interest as both a real estate opportunity and a rare piece of Louisville history. At almost 140 years old, the Speed Mansion is a reminder of how private homes can become places with a much wider cultural legacy.Image Courtesy: Sotheby'sReady to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Gloria Steinem: An icon of American feminism
articles.summary: The trailblazing feminist spoke out for the legalisation of abortion, same-sex marriage and equal pay for women - but her activism was not without backlash.
articles.body:
Gloria Steinem was a powerful icon of America's feminist movement, and her career spanned numerous roles that changed the lives of generations of women.

With her iconic aviator sunglasses and long, blonde-streaked hair - which she considered rebellious in the 1970s - Steinem was an internationally recognised activist in the fight for women's equality.

She spoke out for the legalisation of abortion, same-sex marriage, and equal rights and pay for women, and protested against the death penalty and female genital mutilation.

Her activism was not without a backlash - from both men and women - and harassment that could be as vulgar as it was intimidating.

Born on 25 March 1934 in Toledo, Ohio, Gloria Steinem did not have an easy childhood.

Her father Leo Steinem was a travelling salesman and, together with her mother Ruth and older sister Susanne, they lived in a caravan, crisscrossing the country.

Leo abandoned the family and moved to California when Steinem was 10 years old, leaving her to care for Ruth who had long suffered with mental illness and had terrifying hallucinations.

As a result, Steinem did not go to school full-time until she was 12 years old.

She would later remark that she had never wanted children because she had already had one - her mother.

In the late 1950s she went to India on a research scholarship, and spent two years in a variety of roles, including helping village women organise non-violent protests against government policies, which sparked her interest in grassroots activism.

Steinem left India and moved to New York City in the early 1960s to start her career as a freelance writer. It was a time when male-dominated newsrooms made it difficult for women to get hard-hitting stories.

Her big break came in 1963, when Steinem went undercover as a Playboy Bunny cocktail waitress and wrote A Bunny's Tale, an exposé for Show magazine detailing the seedy and sexist reality of Hugh Hefner's empire.

As soon as she arrived for the interview, a security guard called out, "Here bunny, bunny, bunny."

Using the fake name Marie, she lied about her age - telling Playboy she was 24 years old when she was actually four years older.

Steinem lifted the lid on the underpaid life of a Bunny, and the physical pain of wearing the high-heels and tight corsets for hours.

Despite the fame - and infamy - that followed, she still found herself struggling to be taken seriously by editors.

Though the Playboy exposé helped land her assignments for the New York Times and New York Magazine, often they were about ladies' stockings and the latest hairstyles.

"To this day when people don't like me they introduce me as a former Bunny, as a put-down," she told the New York Times in 2016. "On the other hand, I did improve the working conditions for those women."

Undaunted, by 1968 Steinem was a columnist for New York Magazine, focusing on progressive social issues and women's rights.

Her article, After Black Power, Women's Liberation brought her national fame, making her the face of the US feminist movement in the 1970s.

"I was the only woman, and after I wrote an abortion article, my [male] friends there said to me: 'Don't get involved with these crazy women. You've worked hard to be taken seriously,'" she told Rachel Cooke for The Guardian in 2011.

In 1972, she launched Ms. magazine with a group of feminist activists. It was the first all-female founded and operated periodical, designed to be an alternative to other women's magazines that typically focused on housekeeping and fashion.

Critics - mainly men - were quick to write it off. News presenter Harry Reasoner said he gave it six months "before they run out of things to say".

The first issue sold out within a week and generated 26,000 subscribers. The magazine is still going today.

In 1978, Steinem wrote one of Ms. magazine's most infamous and widely read essays - If Men Could Menstruate.

Her satirical reflection on how different power, political and economic structures might be if men had menstrual cycles is still referred to in discussions about gender roles.

By the end of her career, Steinem had become a prolific and award-winning writer, penning numerous books including her own memoirs, a biography on Marilyn Monroe and a collection of her own famous quotes in the wryly titled, ‪The Truth Will Set You Free, But First It Will Piss You Off.

Though still considered one of the world's best-known feminist activists, Steinem came to advocacy rather late in life - in her thirties.

At an abortion awareness rally in 1969 where women were sharing their experiences of having abortions, Steinem was encouraged to share her own story about terminating a pregnancy. It had taken place years earlier in London when she was 22 years old, just before going to India.

Abortion was illegal in the UK at the time, unless the woman's mental or physical health was in danger. The doctor took a great risk for Steinem, telling her: "You must promise me two things. First, you will not tell anyone my name. Second, you will do what you want to do with your life."

Nearly 60 years later, Steinem broke one of those promises, when she dedicated her memoir, My Life On The Road, to Dr John Sharpe.

She described that abortion speak-out event as a "light bulb moment" - when she realised the US needed a bigger women's rights movement.

Almost overnight, Steinem became a crusader for abortion rights, calling it "reproductive freedom". The phrase she coined is credited with making the subject more approachable for political discussion and continues to be used in abortion debates.

Steinem organised marches and quickly became a draw at demonstrations, although she admitted later that she found talking to the huge crowds "utterly terrifying".

After Congress failed to pass the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA) in 1970 - legislation granting women equal rights to men - Steinem co-founded the National Women's Political Caucus with fellow feminist leaders and more than 300 women across the US. The group worked to include women in all aspects of political and public life.

The same year, she testified at Senate hearings for the ERA, telling the predominantly male audience: "I have been refused service in public restaurants, ordered out of public gathering places and turned away from apartment rentals all for the clearly stated, sole reason that I am a woman."

Second-wave feminism continued to gain momentum and Steinem was one of its most famous figureheads.

She was also supportive of same-sex marriage, but was criticised for an essay she wrote in 1977 on transgender people. She clarified her position in 2013, saying the words in her "old essay" had been taken "out of time and context".

"I believe that transgender people, including those who have transitioned, are living out real, authentic lives. Those lives should be celebrated, not questioned," she wrote in an opinion piece .

Steinem was also criticised for a 1998 essay in the New York Times, where she showed support for then-President Bill Clinton after news broke of his scandalous affair with intern Monica Lewinsky - who was 22 years old at the time.

"The truth is that even if the allegations are true, the president is not guilty of sexual harassment," Steinem wrote. "He is accused of having made a gross, dumb and reckless pass at a supporter during a low point in her life."

In 2017, she said she "wouldn't write the same thing now".

Critics came from the left as well as right, targeting Steinem for everything from her looks to her motives. Some claimed she was too glamorous to be a true feminist, while others said she was successful only because of her appearance.

Betty Friedan, author of The Feminine Mystique, the book credited with launching second-wave feminism , was annoyed that Steinem became the face of the movement, accusing her of "ripping off the movement for private profit" when she launched Ms.

The media were trying "to make her a celebrity," fumed Friedan, "but no one should mistake her for a leader."

US President Richard Nixon was recorded during a secret conversation furiously ranting about Steinem, to which she responded: "There is some opinion that Richard Nixon is the most sexually insecure chief of state since Napoleon".

Al Goldstein, the notorious pornographer and publisher of Screw magazine, launched a campaign of attacks that included publishing her phone number next to fake advertisements for oral sex.

He also printed a graphic centrefold image of a Steinem look-alike, and hung it open on display at the newsstand outside Ms. magazine's office building. She had to look at it every day.

As she got older, harassment to this degree became less common. However, given she was a recognisable figure in New York City, it was not uncommon for Steinem to be stopped on the street by strangers wanting to debate - sometimes with an edge of hostility.

But she welcomed the continued debate. In 2020, she was among a cross-section of public figures who signed an open letter denouncing cancel culture, saying it weakens open debate by shutting people down.

"If you care about having the conversation, surely you want to try in a humane way to convince the other person, not do away with them," she told the New York Times.

Gloria Steinem once quipped: "I can't mate in captivity" - a reference to her disinterest in marriage. But she publicly enjoyed a healthy dating life with a number of rich and famous bachelors, giving critics more ammunition to use against her.

They included Frank Thomas who was head of the Ford Foundation; film director Mike Nichols and Olympic decathlete Rafer Johnson (who helped tackle the man who assassinated Robert F Kennedy in 1968).

"I was the one always accused of using men, of being too sexual. Someone once sent me a cartoon of a tombstone that said 'at last she sleeps alone'," she wrote.

But in 2000, aged 66, she wed David Bale, a South African-born entrepreneur-environmentalist, and father of actor Christian Bale.

At the time, the union drew gasps of surprise and even disappointment from some feminists, who had spent years following Steinem's heated debates surrounding marriage laws.

But she said those laws had finally changed. "If I had married when I was supposed to get married, I would have lost my name, my legal residence, my credit rating, many of my civil rights. That's not true anymore. It's possible to make an equal marriage," she explained years later.

Steinem also confessed to it being a "green card marriage" because Bale's US visa was running out - but said that they loved each other and were going to be together regardless.

Bale died three years later from brain lymphoma.

Steinem had her own health scare with breast cancer in 1986, and underwent a lumpectomy.

Gloria Steinem once said she wanted to live to 100 because "there's so much to do".

In her near-century of life, she even became a talented tap dancer.

She was given America's highest civilian honour - the Presidential Medal of Freedom - in 2013 by President Barack Obama, who credited her work with giving more women "the respect and opportunities that they deserve".

In 2024, she reached the age of 90. She lived alone in New York, content in the knowledge that Ms. Magazine was still publishing.

Steinem seized the occasion to tell the BBC that she hoped her legacy "might help individual people... to become more the unique, valuable, loved and lovable person that they want to be."

She will be remembered for amplifying the voices of women in a way that mainstream media at the time either could not, or would not.

And, in so doing, she altered the landscape and language of women's rights in America.

articles.title: WWE NXT women's champion Kelani Jordan explains why her Heatwave bout was 'one of the best matches' this year
articles.summary: Kelani Jordan calls her NXT Heatwave title win over Kendal Grey one of the best women's matches of the year after a grueling 23-minute bout.
articles.body: Kelani Jordan defeated Kendal Grey for the NXT Women’s Championship at Heatwave and on Tuesday she described the title bout as "one of the best matches of the year" or at least the best "women’s match of the day." It was truly one of the best women’s matches on WWE programming this year. The match lasted nearly 23 minutes and saw Jordan and Grey go blow-for-blow before Grey fell into an exposed turnbuckle and Jordan hit a split-legged moonsault to help seal the win. COMPLETE PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE ON OUTKICK Jordan explained to OutKick Dropkick why she believed their match was one of the best. "Well, first off, Kendal and I, we've always had great chemistry from very early on. I think what makes that match so different than any other match, not that other girls aren't competitive, but Kendal and I are perfectionists, so we both want to give our all. We both give 110%. We both want to win. So, I just feel like that match was very competitive. It was a lot of intensity throughout the whole thing," Jordan said, adding that she believed it was one of the longest NXT women’s singles matches without a stipulation in its history. "So that just speaks for itself. But yeah, I think Kendal and I, we have similar minds." Jordan won the title in her first opportunity. She’s previously held the NXT Women’s North American Championship and the Total Nonstop Action Wrestling (TNA) Knockouts Championship. SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS But to be the champion in the division she’s risen through meant a lot to her. "It feels awesome. It's been a long time coming," she said. "Three and a half years chasing this title. And of course, I had other titles along the way, but this being the top, top, top, top women's title, it feels good. "And also, I went into Heatwave with a chip on my shoulder, knowing that I've been working so hard and that I earned it. articles.title: Kyrgyzstan hosts pivotal SCO summit amid global geopolitical shifts
articles.summary: Kyrgyzstan balances ties with global powers while leveraging its geography to secure economic and political opportunities.
articles.body:
Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan – It was a round table of some of the most influential men in the world. Representing Russia, China, India, Iran, Pakistan – and when they extended to the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Plus – Turkiye, as well as the United Nations Secretary-General, Antonio Guterres. Gathered here in Kyrgyzstan were countries at the centre of some of the world’s biggest geopolitical tensions.

What brings them together is not necessarily agreement on everything. It is the space to pursue their interests outside a Western-led framework. Moscow sees that space as evidence of a changing world.

“Over the 25 years since its inception, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation has evolved into one of the independent and influential centres of the emerging multipolar world,” Russian President Vladimir Putin told the summit.

The organisation, he said, had grown from six founding members in 2001 into what he described as the world’s largest regional association.

Kyrgyzstan is a small, mountainous, landlocked country with Russia to the north and China next door. The calculation is more immediate: how do you balance between giants?

As Europe and the United States are increasingly looking towards Central Asia, Kyrgyzstan needs to balance relations with all of them.

Shairbek Dzhuraev, president of the Crossroads Central Asia think tank, said the timing of the summit is particularly important.

“The members in the room are precisely heavyweights that are directly involved in key geopolitical conflicts of the day,” he said.

That balancing act is not new. Since independence in 1991, Central Asian states have largely operated through what is known as a multi-vector foreign policy.

Bishkek – like other Central Asian nations – operates by keeping Russia close and building ties with China, while keeping open doors to Europe and maintaining healthy relations with Washington.

For Kyrgyzstan, it is less about choosing sides than keeping options open, underscored by its geography. Being landlocked means dependence on transport corridors and being mountainous makes infrastructure more difficult. Dependence on imported energy and external markets leaves the economy exposed to shocks beyond its borders.

“The biggest weakness of Kyrgyzstan, geopolitically and geographically, is the dependence in terms of transport routes, in terms of energy, in terms of economic relationships”, Dzhuraev puts it bluntly.

So diversification becomes more than an economic ambition. Kyrgyzstan, being one of the smaller members, cannot dictate the SCO’s agenda. But it helped to shape the language.

For decades, Central Asia was viewed largely through the prism of the powers surrounding it. But the wars in the region and beyond have changed that – Russia is under sanctions, so is Iran, China is looking west, Europe is looking east. Suddenly the geography has acquired new value with highways, railways, pipelines, trade corridors, power networks and the periphery is becoming a strategically important passageway. Dzhuraev said: “Kyrgyzstan wanted the summit declaration to recognise that transformation, Central Asia’s movement into the centre stage of international politics”.

The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation is increasingly seen as a counterweight to US influence — a grouping through which China and Russia can advance a different vision of the global order. But the SCO is too diverse for a simple East-versus-West confrontation. That description comes with a qualification that the SCO is not a unified anti-American bloc.

Its members have competing interests, different relationships with Washington and, in some cases, deep disagreements with one another. The question is not whether the SCO rejects the West, it is whether it can resist being defined entirely in opposition to it.

Iran brings that to the centre stage – where geopolitical theory meets a much more immediate crisis. Tehran and Washington have returned to confrontation after more than a month of relative calm. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian used the SCO summit to put the diplomatic question directly on the table.

“I state explicitly that if the United States returns to its commitments under the aforementioned memorandum of understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately take reciprocal action,” he said.

The Islamabad MoU signed in June collapsed, with Tehran and Washington blaming each other for violating its terms. Iran’s Foreign Minister, Abbas Araghchi, also called on Washington to return to what its president signed under the MoU. “In that case, everything can be put back on the right track,” he said.

For the SCO, however, Iran is not simply a diplomatic issue – it is an economic one. Washington has renewed sanctions on Tehran and expanded the threat of penalties for those doing business with Iran. For Central Asia, that matters, particularly for countries whose economies are deeply intertwined with Russia and increasingly connected to Chinese trade networks. Dzhuraev is sceptical whether countries such as Kyrgyzstan comply fully with sanctions, “The declaration will most likely not match the reality,” he said. “China and other countries have already rejected what they describe as unilateral sanctions.”

The reality is that sanctions can hurt, as they have hurt Iran and Russia. Not as intended for economic collapse, but they brought pain for the masses and put a spanner in their economies. But enforcement across a region built around cross-border trade is another matter. For Central Asian economies, complete compliance is difficult because the economic relationships are too dense, which is quite different from Western compliance. Both with Iran and Russia, transport and trade links have been growing steadily, so countries are unlikely to simply switch them off overnight.

That makes the SCO summit an important political moment.

Not necessarily because its members can defeat the sanctions regime, but because they can collectively signal where they stand on unilateral pressure.

When you speak to delegates from the global south, there is also a broader message: that the SCO is becoming a forum where countries that do not necessarily agree on everything can nevertheless agree on one principle: they want room to manoeuvre.

Putin calls that the emergence of a multipolar world, Pezeshkian is using the forum to keep diplomacy with Washington alive on Iran’s terms, China is defending its economic relationships, India is pursuing its own strategic interests, and Kyrgyzstan is trying to make sure none of these relationships closes the door to another.

But there is a second question confronting Kyrgyzstan — and it is not sitting around the summit table. How much of its rise belongs to Kyrgyzstan itself?

As transit trade has risen, the economy has been growing rapidly, wages have increased, construction has accelerated and exports have increased.

There is visible momentum in Bishkek, with new roads and buildings appearing to fill the empty spaces. Extraordinary circumstances have generated a lot, such as the war in Ukraine, which has altered regional trade and expanded Chinese investment. When trade routes shifted, money and demand moved across borders. The government is proud that much of the recent development has been undertaken without the external borrowing that characterised earlier periods. But buildings alone do not create a productive economy. External momentum can be a dangerous foundation for long-term growth, as Dzhuraev points out. “Productivity is growing. Exports are rising. More goods are being produced domestically. But much of the momentum remains connected to external factors — particularly the Russia-Ukraine war and Chinese investment. One of the biggest drivers of poverty reduction has been rising salaries.”

The harder question is what comes next? Where are the productive sectors that will sustain those incomes? Agriculture could be an obvious answer as Kyrgyzstan is an agricultural country. But glaciers are melting and climate change is having an impact. Plus, its long-term capacity to generate higher-value growth remains uncertain. That may ultimately be the more important story behind this summit. Not the speeches, the flags, nor the declaration.

Kyrgyzstan wants to convert geography into leverage and its vulnerabilities into options. But the wider questions remain, whether Central Asia can move from being the space between Russia, China, Iran and Europe to becoming a centre of its own? As well as whether today’s economic growth can survive when the external forces driving it inevitably change?

Kyrgyzstan finds itself at the centre of a changing region that brings opportunity but also pressure. Between the giants, keeping every door open may be the most important strategy of all.

articles.title: Kenya's President William Ruto orders crackdown on foreigners operating small businesses
articles.summary: It comes amid concerns over the growing number of traders from neighbouring countries.
articles.body:
Kenya's President William Ruto has ordered a crackdown on foreigners operating small-scale businesses, saying local traders and hawkers need to be protected.

His announcement comes amid growing debate about the increasing number of African migrants involved in Kenya's vast informal economy.

"From next week, all [foreign] traders doing those small businesses should close them," he said, also promising to fast-track proposed legislation to preclude foreigners from certain areas of trade.

Ruto said Kenya remained open to foreign investment, but argued that investors - including Chinese traders - should create jobs and expand production rather than compete with Kenyans in small businesses.

"It cannot be that a person comes from China or elsewhere to be a hawker or open a small shop," he said in an address to small-scale traders who had come to meet the president at State House in the capital, Nairobi, on Wednesday afternoon.

"We have made efforts to improve the economy, we have not improved investor confidence for hawkers to come to Kenya," said Ruto, who plans to seek a second term in election next year.

It is unclear how many foreign nationals are involved in small-scale trading or how many would be affected by the new crackdown.

Kenya hosts a large refugee population, some of whom live and work outside the country's refugee camps.

Government figures show that Kenya had about 857,000 registered refugees and asylum seekers by the end of June, with nearly 14% living in urban areas.

Kenyan law recognises the right of refugees to work and operate businesses, although they are required to obtain the appropriate documentation. Refugees wishing to work or engage in a trade or business can apply for a special permit.

In Nairobi and other major towns, migrants from the region can be found working in barber shops and salons, construction, operating motorbike taxis and street vending, as well as selling clothes, food and household goods.

Some have fled conflicts or economic hardship at home, while others have moved to Kenya in search of better opportunities under the relatively free movement of people allowed within the East African Community, a regional bloc made up of eight countries.

The growing presence of foreigners has at times caused tensions with local traders and workers who accuse them of competing for scarce jobs and business opportunities.

In July, a video of a Kenyan man confronting a Burundian trader in Nairobi and accusing him of taking opportunities from locals sparked widespread criticism.

The clash also prompted Fred Ngoga, an expert on regional conflict prevention from Burundi, to appeal for the protection of his country's citizens.

"The majority of Kenyans are decent and good people who welcome their brothers and sisters from Burundi," he said at the time, adding that most Kenyans had rejected the hostility directed at the trader.

Kenya's foreign ministry also sought to reassure Burundians and other East Africans living in the country following the incident.

While Ruto's latest move is likely to prove controversial given Kenya's status as regional economic hub, it also comes amid wider concerns about xenophobia elsewhere in Africa.

This year South Africa has seen a wave of protests about undocumented migrants - and tens of thousands of Africans there have opted to be repatriated voluntarily, some saying they have been the targets of intimidation and attacks.

articles.title: Rust streaks, faded paint and 5,000 tired sailors: War-weary USS Lincoln docks in Thailand
articles.summary: International News: A rusted and worn USS Abraham Lincoln arrived in Thailand after an extraordinary 286 days of deployment at sea. The carrier shows visible signs of wea.
articles.body: A rusted and worn USS Abraham Lincoln arrived in Thailand after an extraordinary 286 days of deployment at sea. The carrier shows visible signs of wear and tear, its hull streaked with rust and its paint visibly weathered after months of combat and blockade operations in the Middle East.The appearance of the US Navy's nuclear-powered aircraft carrier serves as a visual record of its extended deployment and long overdue need for maintenance.Naval experts say prolonged exposure to seawater, humidity and heavy operational activity can leave even major warships visibly weathered when there is little opportunity for routine preservation work.The Lincoln, which carries roughly 5,000 sailors and Marines, entered Laem Chabang port on Wednesday after leaving its homeport of San Diego on November 21, 2025.The carrier had spent much of its deployment in the Middle East, where it participated in US operations against Iran, including naval blockade and combat missions.Its Thailand port call is expected to last four to five days, giving personnel their first significant opportunity for rest and recuperation after the marathon deployment.286 days at seaUS naval deployments typically last between six and nine months, although they can be extended considerably during wartime.The Lincoln's deployment stretched far beyond that norm. According to reporting by Reuters, the carrier had one uninterrupted stretch of around 208 days at sea, described as a modern-era operational record by Democratic lawmakers.Its strike group was eventually relieved by the USS George Washington, allowing the Lincoln to begin its return journey.The prolonged deployment placed considerable demands on the carrier and its accompanying vessels. Reuters photographs showed not only the Lincoln but also the guided-missile destroyer USS Frank E. Petersen Jr. and cruiser USS Robert Smalls with visible rust and mottled paint around their waterlines.That suggests the deterioration was not unique to the carrier but part of the broader wear accumulated by ships operating continuously in a harsh maritime environment.Carl Schuster, a former US Navy captain who served aboard Nimitz-class carriers, told CNN that rust along the waterline was not unusual after extended periods at sea. Removing it requires crews to work close to the waterline, sand away corrosion and apply multiple layers of protective coating, work that is difficult to undertake while a ship is actively deployed.Rust itself does not establish a loss of combat capability, but corrosion control requires time, manpower and maintenance capacity. The longer such work is deferred during operations, the greater the maintenance burden once a ship returns to port.The weathered appearance of the Lincoln comes amid broader questions about the strain imposed by its unusually long deployment.Reuters reported that the ship had faced allegations of deteriorating conditions, supply shortages and mental-health concerns among its crew. Some families and lawmakers raised concerns about food and hygiene supplies, plumbing, laundry and communication during the prolonged mission.The Pentagon has disputed some of those accounts. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth previously said reports about conditions aboard the carrier had been misrepresented, while Admiral Brad Cooper said after visiting the ship that it had among the lowest mental-health case numbers across the Navy's 11 carriers.The competing accounts underline a larger problem: sustaining a warship in combat is not simply a question of whether its weapons and aircraft remain operational.A carrier also requires thousands of people, regular supplies, spare parts, maintenance and opportunities for its crew to recover.Rear Admiral Robert Loughran, commander of Carrier Strike Group Three, described the Thailand visit as an opportunity for sailors and Marines to "rest and recharge" after what he called "truly historic" accomplishments.The Lincoln's deployment also illustrates how the war with Iran has stretched US naval resources across theatres.Every additional day that a carrier remains deployed provides sustained American military presence, but also adds to maintenance requirements and keeps a scarce high-end naval asset away from other potential theatres.The Lincoln's relief by another carrier demonstrates the rotational depth needed to maintain continuous US naval presence during prolonged conflicts.Its arrival in Thailand is a visible reminder of the logistical network required to keep American carrier groups operating thousands of miles from home.The Thailand visit will not include a joint military exercise, with the focus instead on rest and recuperation.Sailors and Marines have begun heading to Pattaya, around 150 km from Laem Chabang, where local businesses are expecting an economic boost from the thousands of US personnel.Thailand has been a US treaty ally since 1954, and American military vessels have long made port calls in the country.

And the Los Angeles Clippers are handed one of steepest penalties in NBA history. Here’s what to know today. White House moves to make the midterms about Trump In a meeting last week, some of President Donald Trump’s senior advisers were told by his pollster that the midterms outlook for Republicans is grim, according to a person familiar with the discussion. Republican voters aren’t all that enthused about November’s elections in which Trump isn’t on the ballot, the advisers were told. It’s not a good sign for the GOP, which is fighting to maintain its thin majorities in the House and Senate. So, in a bid to bolster voter turnout, the administration is looking for ways to make the midterms about Trump. One approach is telling any and all disaffected voters that the president has answers to the economic anxieties that people face, which could be tough considering the ongoing Iran war and the high prices — especially for diesel fuel — that have resulted. A second approach is rousing Trump’s core supporters to get them to show up as if he’s on the ballot. Next week, Trump will appear at a first-of-its-kind GOP midterm campaign event in Dallas. And he is planning to hit the campaign trail in the weeks leading up to the election for Republican candidates in 35 races. But a Trump-centric strategy is a gamble. articles.summary: News News: Home sales in Canada's Greater Toronto Area fell in August for the first time in six months as concerns over trade and the possibility of higher borro.
articles.body: Home sales in Canada's Greater Toronto Area fell in August for the first time in six months as concerns over trade and the possibility of higher borrowing costs prompted some buyers to hold off, data from the Toronto Regional Real Estate Board showed on Thursday.Seasonally adjusted home sales declined 1.3% in August from July to 5,484 units, ending a run of monthly gains that had continued since March.The board's seasonally adjusted home price index edged down 0.1% month-on-month to C$931,200 ($672,784).Trade concerns and borrowing costs weigh on buyers“The main hold-back for many households has been concerns around trade with the United States and the potential for higher inflation and borrowing costs in the future,” Jason Mercer, the board's chief information officer, said in a statement, as cited by Reuters.The Bank of Canada on Wednesday kept its key policy rate unchanged at 2.25%. However, Governor Tiff Macklem said policymakers were prepared to raise borrowing costs multiple times if inflation remained too high.The housing data also comes after the United States imposed new 50% tariffs last month on $20 billion worth of Canadian imports following the collapse of talks between the two countries.Sales and prices decline from a year earlierOn a year-on-year basis, home sales in the Greater Toronto Area fell 2.1% in August, while new listings declined 14.1%.The board's home price index was also down 4.5% from a year earlier.The Greater Toronto Area includes Canada's most populous city, Toronto, along with four surrounding regional municipalities.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Driver admits killing Keaton Slater in Coventry hit-and-run crash
articles.summary: Dolars Aleksanders' car hit Keaton Slater, 12, as he made his way home from school in Coventry.
articles.body:
A man has admitted causing death by dangerous driving after a 12-year-old boy died in a hit-and-run crash as he made his way home from school.

Latvian national Dolars Aleksanders was extradited to the UK last month, following the death of Keaton Slater in Coventry in 2024.

The 23-year-old appeared at Warwick Crown Court via a virtual link from HMP Dovegate and spoke only to enter his guilty plea. He is due to be sentenced on 13 November.

Keaton's parents said they had had to endure the heartbreak of losing their son, while also fighting for accountability. They said Aleksanders' extradition and plea meant "justice" for Keaton.

Judge Matthew Walsh told the defendant: "You have entered your guilty plea to this very serious matter.

"Plainly the sentence that you are going to have imposed upon you is to be a very long one.

"That will be determined by Her Honour Judge [Kristina] Montgomery KC."

It comes after Aleksanders struck the Coventry schoolboy with his black BMW 330 on Radford Road on 14 June 2024.

At the time of the incident, West Midlands Police said there were four people in the car, which was driving "well above" the speed limit when it hit Keaton.

A reward of £10,000 was also offered up by Crimestoppers for information that led to Aleksanders' arrest.

It was later discovered that the defendant had fled to Latvia where efforts to extradite him started soon after he was named by police as a person of interest.

After evading West Midlands Police for more than two years, he was flown into Gatwick Airport last month and was then transported to a custody block in the West Midlands.

Crown Prosecution Service spokesman Ben Samples said British and Latvian authorities, as well as international agencies, had worked closely together to "bring Mr Aleksanders back to face proceedings in a UK court".

Keaton's parents, Louise and Clint Slater, were sitting in the public gallery of the court as Aleksanders entered his plea.

In a statement, the family said: "For two years, we have struggled to come to terms with Keaton's death while also having to live with the devastating feeling that justice has not been done.

"We have had to endure the heartbreak of losing our son while waiting, hoping and fighting for accountability."

They added that there had been times when the pain had "felt unbearable" and days when it had been "difficult to see a way forward".

"But today, after two long and heartbreaking years, we can finally say that justice has been done for Keaton," they said.

"Nothing will ever bring our beautiful boy back. No sentence, no outcome and no words can ever take away the pain of losing him.

"But finally having justice means that Keaton's life and the circumstances surrounding his death have been acknowledged.

"We will never stop loving Keaton. We will never stop missing him. And we will never stop speaking his name.

"Keaton was more than the way he died. He was our son, our beautiful boy, and a huge part of our lives. He will always be remembered, always be loved, and always be in our hearts."

Det Ch Insp Sam Lewis, who led the investigation, said: "This has always been about getting justice for Keaton and his family.

"Keaton should have had his life ahead of him, but the selfish and reckless actions of Aleksanders took this away from him.

"Aleksanders was speeding at an excessive level and would have known the impact of the collision.

"He could have sought to help Keaton but instead fled, leaving him to die and his family to deal with an unimaginable amount of grief and pain.

"Everyone that has heard Keaton's story has been determined to do everything possible to catch the person responsible.

"This has been a complex investigation but we've always remained resolute and bonded by the belief that we would ensure Aleksanders was convicted for his appalling actions."

In 2025, Coventry City Council announced a reduced speed limit of 20mph would be imposed on Radford Road where Keaton had been hit.

Taiwo Owatemi, MP for Coventry North West, described his death as "heartbreaking" but said she was proud the city council had responded to a petition made in his name.

articles.title: Honoring the ‘butcher of Bosnia’ would be a crude endorsement of genocide
articles.summary: Despite overwhelming evidence to the contrary, Bosnian Serb and Serbian leaders continue to deny that the genocide happened.
articles.body:
The death of General Radko Mladic is a reminder of the worst genocide in Europe since the Holocaust and the need to remember it. Unfortunately, the governments of the Bosnian Serb Republic and Serbia proper continue to deny what happened.

The Serbian Minister of Justice announced that Mladic will be buried with the “highest military and state honors.” Dubbed “the butcher of Bosnia,” Mladic oversaw Serb military operations during the civil war of the early 1990s, including the July 1995 massacre of up to 8,000 Muslim men and boys in the town of Srebrenica .

Along with Bosnian Serb President Radovan Karadzic and Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic, he implemented a policy of ethnic cleansing — the removal of Muslims and Croats from land claimed by Serbs. Through rape, murder and brutality, the Bosnian Serb Army and paramilitary forces from Serbia drove thousands of people from their homes. Based on careful analysis of data, the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia estimated the death toll at 89,186, of whom 57,922 were Bosnian Muslims, most of them civilians.

Following the signing of the Dayton Peace Accords in December 1995, the tribunal pursued the perpetrators, especially the three Serbian leaders.

It indicted Milosevic in 1999 and began trying him in 2002 following his arrest in Serbia, but he died in 2006 before the tribunal could render a verdict. It convicted Karadzic of “genocide, crimes against humanity and violations of the laws or customs of war committed by Serb forces,” of which he was supreme commander. He is currently serving a 40-year sentence in the Hague. Mladic eluded authorities for 16 years before Serbian authorities arrested him in 2011. The tribunal found him guilty of “”genocide, crimes against humanity and violations of the laws or customs of war” in 2017 and sentenced him to life in prison.

Despite overwhelming evidence to the contrary, Bosnian Serb and Serbian leaders continue to deny that the genocide had happened. Milorad Dodik, Bosnian Serb Republic president from 2022 to 2025, called the genocide a “fabricated myth” and commissioned a report to promulgate his baseless argument.

Aleksandar Vucic, president of Serbia since 2017, has been a consistent genocide denier . He and many of his followers insist that since all sides committed atrocities, no one is guilty . That argument sounds remarkably similar to the one used by the government of Turkey to deny responsibility for the 1915 Armenian genocide .

In April 2024, thousands of Bosnian Serbs attended a rally in Banja Luka to deny that the Srebrenica massacre occurred.

To the outside observer two questions immediately occur: Why the denial, and what does it matter? Nationalists blend fact and fiction to create patriotic myths . Victimhood permeates the Serbian historical narrative. It contains a litany of wrongs done to the Serbian people but no acknowledgement of what they have done to others.

Their leaders refuse to acknowledge the Bosnian genocide, just as some American politicians downplay the evils of slavery and the removal of Native Americans. It matters for the same reason denial of the Armenian genocide and the Holocaust matter: Such denial increases the likelihood that such tragedies will happen again.

On the eve of the invasion of Poland, a war in which he promised to kill “mercilessly and without compassion, men, women, and children of Polish derivation and language,” Adolf Hitler quipped , “Who, after all, speaks of the annihilation of the Armenians?”

After World War II, the Jewish people adopted the slogan “ never again ” as a commitment to oppose genocide whenever and wherever it threatened to occur. A corollary to that declaration must be “never forget.” As the tragedy of Bosnia recedes into the past and remembrance fades, it may cease to serve as a stark warning of what human beings driven by hatred and ethnic nationalism can do.

To prevent that happening, the United Nations General Assembly designated July 11 as “International Day of Reflection and Commemoration of the 1995 Genocide in Srebrenica, to be observed annually.” The UN resolution also condemned denying the genocide and glorifying its perpetrators.

Burying Mladic with full military honors violates that resolution and every code of human decency. The funeral dishonors the victims and, as one Serbian journalist concluded, traps the Serbian people in the past instead of moving them toward reconciliation.

Tom Mockaitis is a professor of history at DePaul University and the author of “ Violent Extremists: Understanding the Domestic and International Terrorist Threat .”

articles.title: A San Francisco bystander heard screams from a garbage truck after its load had been compacted; 25 firefighters spent more than 2 hours digging a trapped man out alive
articles.summary: US News: A routine garbage collection in San Francisco turned into a desperate rescue early Wednesday after a bystander heard screams coming from inside a garb.
articles.body: A routine garbage collection in San Francisco turned into a desperate rescue early Wednesday after a bystander heard screams coming from inside a garbage truck. The San Francisco Fire Department responded at about 4:11 a.m. on September 2, after the passerby alerted the Recology driver that someone appeared to be yelling from the vehicle. By then, the truck's load had already been compacted, leaving a man trapped beneath a large amount of garbage. According to PEOPLE and FOX 32 Chicago, around 25 firefighters spent more than two hours carefully removing the waste by hand to reach him. The man remained conscious and communicative during the rescue and was eventually taken to Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital in serious condition.Screams trigger emergency responseThe incident unfolded on Mason Street near San Francisco's Union Square, close to the Powell BART station. A bystander heard what sounded like a person shouting from inside the garbage truck and stopped the Recology driver. The driver then contacted emergency services, bringing firefighters to the scene shortly after 4 a.m. When firefighters assessed the truck, they realised they were dealing with an unusually difficult rescue. A person was trapped somewhere beneath the garbage that had already been collected and compacted. The situation meant that simply emptying the truck was not considered safe. Instead, firefighters had to figure out how to remove the garbage while protecting the person buried underneath it.Firefighters remove trash by handAbout 25 firefighters took part in the rescue operation, which continued for more than two hours. Rather than relying on the truck's normal unloading process, crews manually removed garbage from the vehicle. Large amounts of waste were taken out and spread across the street as firefighters worked toward the trapped man.The rescue was complicated by the fact that the victim was underneath a substantial amount of refuse. Firefighters feared that dumping the contents all at once could further injure him, so they removed the garbage carefully while working toward his location. Despite the circumstances, the man remained conscious and able to communicate with rescuers. Paramedics also provided medical care while firefighters continued working to free him. Medical team feared crush syndromeThe man's condition made the rescue particularly urgent. According to PEOPLE, paramedics administered an intravenous line to help prevent crush syndrome, a potentially dangerous medical condition that can occur after a person has been trapped under heavy pressure for an extended period. When pressure is released, damaged muscle tissue can release substances into the bloodstream that may cause serious complications. The medical team therefore had to consider not only the man's immediate injuries but also what could happen when he was finally removed from the garbage. Firefighters eventually reached and extracted him before 7 a.m., ending a rescue that had lasted several hours from the initial emergency call.Man hospitalised after rescueThe rescued man was taken to Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital in serious condition, a spokesperson said, according to The San Francisco Standard. Authorities were also investigating how he ended up inside the garbage truck. Officials believed the man had likely been inside a dumpster before it was emptied into the truck. A mechanical collection system lifts dumpsters and transfers their contents into the vehicle, creating the possibility that someone inside a container could be carried into the truck without being noticed. Recology spokesperson Robert Reed told PEOPLE that such incidents are highly unusual and that the last similar case occurred about 15 years ago.The incident also highlighted the dangers associated with climbing into refuse containers. Once a person is inside a dumpster, there is no guarantee they will be seen before the container is emptied, and garbage trucks can compact their loads with enormous force. For the firefighters on Mason Street, however, the first warning came from a simple sound: someone shouting for help. That bystander's decision to stop the truck and alert the driver ultimately triggered the rescue response. What followed was more than two hours of painstaking work as firefighters emptied a garbage truck piece by piece, searching through its contents until they could reach the trapped man and bring him out alive.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
