articles.title: Decision on 2,400-acre Oxfordshire solar farm plans delayed again
articles.summary: The government delays its decision on the Botley West solar farm proposals until November.
articles.body:
Controversial plans to build one of the UK's largest solar farms have been delayed further by the government, which says it needs additional time to "consider further information".

Developer Photovolt Development Partners (PVDP) wants to build the Botley West Solar Farm across more than 2,000 acres of land to the north and west of Oxford.

A decision on the scheme had been due earlier this year, before being pushed back to September 2026 by then-Energy Secretary Ed Miliband.

In a statement on Wednesday, the government confirmed that its decision on the proposals would now be further postponed until 10 November at the latest.

On the latest setback, Minister for Local Energy and Jobs Martin McCluskey said it would "enable my department and other interested parties to consider further information received from the applicant".

"The decision to set the new deadline for this application is without prejudice to the decision on whether to grant or refuse development consent," he added.

The final decision on the proposals will fall to Miatta Fahnbulleh, who succeeded Miliband as the secretary of state for energy security and net zero in July.

PVDP previously said the project was crucial to meet the UK's climate and energy security goals, and could power the equivalent of 330,000 homes.

If approved, the £800m solar farm would cover about 1,000 hectares (2,471 acres) across three areas - north of Woodstock, west of Kidlington and west of Botley.

Reacting to the latest delay, the developers said it was a "common part" of the process for a project "of this scale and significance".

"The additional time will allow the department to review the further information submitted and ensure all relevant considerations are properly assessed before a decision is reached," the company said.

"We remain confident in the strength of our application, which has been shaped by extensive consultation and detailed environmental and technical assessment."

But the proposals have proved particularly controversial in the local area, with campaigners previously saying the development would harm an 11km (7-mile) rural corridor.

On Wednesday's further delay, the group Stop Botley West said the government was allowing PVDP "even more time to do its homework and answer longstanding challenges".

This, it said, was an "abuse of what should be a strict and fair planning process".

"We know that hundreds of Oxfordshire residents are angered and frustrated by the further delay and feel unfairly let down by a planning system that we've been asked to respect," the group said.

Bicester and Woodstock MP Calum Miller, who has been a vocal opponent of the plans, said the latest postponement "crystallises what was already clear: this Botley West application is full of holes and should be rejected outright".

"The new secretary of state should reject this proposal and back renewable energy schemes that deliver genuine community benefit and respect the places where they are built," he added.

articles.title: India's Modi-Iran meeting comes amid US warnings of sanctions on Tehran's trading partners
articles.summary: Trump administration Iran sanctions threaten India's commercial and energy ties with Tehran, putting India-U.S. relations to the test over secondary sanctions.
articles.body: The Trump administration is ramping up economic sanctions on Iran through "Operation Economic Outcast," while also threatening dire secondary sanctions against countries that continue Iran-related business. The new policy puts countries like India and other close U.S. partners in an awkward situation. New Delhi remains a critical U.S. partner in the Indo-Pacific, but it also has commercial, energy and strategic interests in Iran that it won't likely discard, potentially putting it at odds with the Trump administration. TRUMP THREATENS 'UNPRECEDENTED' ECONOMIC CONSEQUENCES FOR ANY NATION AIDING IRAN On Monday, exactly a week after the Trump administration launched its new sanctions campaign, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi met with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Kyrgyzstan. It was their first meeting since the war broke out six months ago. According to an Iranian readout, Pezeshkian asked Modi "to use India’s extensive contacts" to help steer the involved parties away from war and back toward dialogue, while thanking Modi for standing by Tehran. Modi reiterated that New Delhi wants to strengthen its "long-standing friendship" with Tehran and "expand and diversify" the two countries’ trade basket. "That was for Modi to signal to a domestic audience that he is not kowtowing to Trump," Council on Foreign Relations Senior Fellow Sadanand Dhume told Fox News Digital. "India-Iran relations have already been largely hollowed out by previous rounds of sanctions, so there is no question of India trying to balance between the U.S. and Iran," he added. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was asked by Fox News' Brian Kilmeade on "The Brian Kilmeade Show" Tuesday about Modi's meeting with the Iranian president. Rubio said he didn't think there was a trade deal between India and Iran — noting many countries around the world talk to Tehran — and stated, "What ultimately happens, though, is – and the President’s been very clear – is no country should be helping Iran evade sanctions. No country should be out there helping them create mechanisms by which they can generate revenue that they will then use to sponsor terrorism and try to build a nuclear weapon. And if countries decide to do that, then we’re going to have to sanction them too." A U.S. official echoed Rubio's comments and told Fox News Digital that, "the Administration continues to have positive discussions with our economic partners to ensure Iran never possesses a nuclear weapon." India has been among Iran’s top five trading partners in recent years, though bilateral trade has dropped dramatically since its 2018-19 peak. IRAN LOSES KEY ECONOMIC LIFELINE IN MIDDLE EAST THAT TRUMP'S SANCTIONS COULDN'T REACH AS DEADLOCK PERSISTS New Delhi’s exports to Iran are concentrated on goods that can carry humanitarian exemptions, including pharmaceuticals. Iran is also the second-largest overseas market for Indian rice, with India exporting more than $383 million worth in the first six months of the year. Conversely, India resumed importing Iranian crude oil for the first time in seven years in April, after the Trump administration temporarily lifted sanctions to soften the Middle East conflict’s impact on global energy. Iranian oil shipments to India were valued at roughly $707 million in the first half of the year. India has already come into the Treasury Department's crosshairs, with the U.S. sanctioning four India-based companies and three Indian nationals over alleged links to Iranian petroleum and petrochemical trade. The Treasury Department says countries will receive a defined timeline to shut down Iran-related activity as identified by Washington. That puts banks, shippers, insurers and trade intermediaries on notice before any further penalties are imposed. The United Arab Emirates’ suspension of commercial and financial dealings with Iran has already squeezed Indian exporters, as Dubai has long served as a key hub for trade with Iran. IRAN DEAL CLOCK HITS ZERO AS TRUMP DEMANDS ‘WHITE FLAG’ WITH NEW PRESSURE CAMPAIGN LOOMING So far, Washington’s initial actions have stopped short of targeting India’s wider commercial relationship with Iran. Iran, meanwhile, has warned of "grave consequences" for countries that cooperate with what it calls illegal U.S. behavior. India's interests in Iran also run beyond commerce. The Chabahar port, Iran’s only deep-water oceanic port, provides maritime routes linking India to Russia and Europe. It also gives India an access route to Central Asia that bypasses Pakistan. But U.S. sanctions uncertainty has repeatedly complicated India’s operations there. India, the world's third-biggest oil importer and consumer, has already faced the cost of the Middle East conflict, through energy disruptions, higher import costs and inflation. It has also shown it will resist U.S. pressure when core interests are at stake. For instance, it has defended ties with Russia, despite Moscow’s adversarial relationship with Washington. But experts argue Iran no longer carries the same weight. "The Russian example is strikingly different. New Delhi shares close military and diplomatic ties with Moscow that are much more important to India than its ties with Iran, notwithstanding lip service to the latter," Dhume said. "Higher global oil prices hurt India, but India weaned itself off Iranian oil imports a while back." For the U.S., squeezing major economies like India over their ties to Tehran could pose a diplomatic risk. U.S. national security officials stress the need for a workable strategic relationship with India, especially to counterbalance Chinese power. Under President Trump’s second term, once-blooming US-India relations have been under strain. Trump and Modi sought to reset the relationship just months ago, but the latest Iran sanctions could test it again. But the U.S. retains enormous leverage over India, particularly when it comes to trade. "If forced to choose, New Delhi will obviously and emphatically choose its valuable commercial relationship with the U.S. over its skimpy trade ties with the Islamic republic," Dhume said. The timing is notable, with Chinese President Xi Jinping reportedly set to visit India for next week’s BRICS summit. Russian President Vladimir Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian are also expected to attend. Analysts say the impact will ultimately depend on how aggressively Washington moves from warnings and diplomacy to actual secondary sanctions. That is particularly true with India, where more aggressive enforcement risks further straining U.S. relations with a strategically important partner. "The U.S. should learn from its own past success in quietly persuading India to generally kick its Iran oil habit." Dhume said. "Quiet diplomacy works better with India than bluster. This is the key lesson from the past that the Trump administration appears to be forgetting." articles.title: Dolly Parton gets new star on Hollywood Walk of Fame after vandalism
articles.summary: Fans laid flowers on the singer's star after her death, but vandals scratched her name off.
articles.body:
Dolly Parton's star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame has been replaced after the original one was vandalised following the late country legend's death last week.

Fans had laid flowers and left candles around her star in the heart of Hollywood, Los Angeles, which was awarded in 1984.

But on Monday, photos showed it had been damaged after vandals scratched it, leaving her name badly defaced.

Repairs were carried out on Wednesday, and the Hollywood Historic Trust said the new star will be unveiled on Friday.

"The Hollywood Historic Trust and Hollywood Chamber of Commerce are proud to honour the legacy of Dolly Parton with a replacement of her star," the organisation wrote on Instagram on Wednesday.

"The new star will be available for viewing this Friday."

Ana Martinez of the Hollywood Chamber of Commerce said the tribute items left on the star had been cleared before the work, which had already been planned to repair cracks before it was vandalised.

The Hollywood Walk of Fame is a landmark with more than 2,800 stars embedded along Hollywood Boulevard.

It marks the achievements of individuals and groups across the entertainment industry.

Tributes poured in from around the music world and beyond after Parton, known for hits including 9 to 5 and Jolene, died last week at the age of 80.

The singer-songwriter was laid to rest next to her late husband Carl Dean at a private family funeral in Nashville on Friday.

The following evening, one of Parton's nieces, Jada Star, performed as part of a tribute concert at Nashville's Grand Ole Opry House, regarded as the home of country music.

Elsewhere, Parton's theme park Dollywood has announced several new features to honour its "dreamer-in-chief".

The singer and actress purchased the Tennessee attraction in 1982, seeing it as a counterpart to Disneyland.

It has since become the biggest ticketed tourist attraction in Tennessee, receiving about four million visitors per year.

A waterfall will be added outside the chapel's front steps, creating a "peaceful setting for guests to pause, reflect and enjoy the natural beauty" of the area, a statement said .

The chapel will also have new stained-glass windows to reflect one of Parton's favourite Bible verses: "For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven."

Also, to honour Parton's love of children and her Imagination Library book donation programme, the park will introduce a new character called the Dream Maker next year.

articles.title: UN warns El Nino could be ‘off the charts’, strongest in decades
articles.summary: The World Meteorological Organization says forecasts show 100% likelihood that El Nino will continue through February.
articles.body:
El Nino is set to intensify to exceptional levels in the coming months and persist into early 2027, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) has warned, raising the prospect of worsening droughts, floods and extreme heat across the globe.

The United Nations weather agency said on Thursday forecasts show a nearly 100 percent likelihood that El Nino will continue through February, the strongest level of certainty it has ever expressed in an El Nino/La Nina update.

The naturally occurring weather phenomenon warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns.

“If this trajectory continues, it may be stronger than anything since our monitoring began – so literally off the charts we have used for the past four decades,” WMO chief Celeste Saulo told reporters in Geneva, Switzerland. El Nino will peak towards the end of this year, though its knock-on impacts for the climate will continue well into 2027, said the WMO.

Heat in the oceans releases more slowly into the atmosphere, pushing up global temperatures the following year.

The powerful 2023-24 El Nino contributed to 2024 being the warmest year on record, and “we should not be surprised if this record is broken”, Saulo said.

“El Nino is firmly established and will intensify into a very strong event in the coming months, with big impacts on rainfall and temperature patterns and associated risks of floods, drought and extreme heat,” the WMO said.

El Nino is a natural phenomenon and is not caused by climate change. But scientists expect it will exacerbate the heat of a planet already warming as a result of burning fossil fuels, while amping up weather extremes.

“El Nino is being supersized before our eyes,” said UN chief Antonio Guterres. “The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up. Sea surface temperatures are rising, temperatures keep climbing, and the world is in the danger zone of extreme weather.

“The race now is between rising risks and our commitment to take climate action and protect people. We must win that race.”

“This exceptional El Nino … has the potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world,” Saulo said.

“We are already seeing disruption and devastation from droughts and floods, and we expect these impacts to increase as El Nino intensifies.”

She put disaster management authorities and climate-sensitive sectors like agriculture, healthcare, energy and water on notice, saying there was “no time to lose” in getting ready.

El Nino typically takes place every two to seven years and lasts nine months to a year.

Conditions oscillate between El Nino and its opposite La Nina, with neutral conditions in between.

“Fuelled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific, El Nino is expected to strengthen further during the coming months to a very strong intensity,” the WMO said.

The UN agency classifies El Nino events as weak, moderate, strong or very strong – meaning it is set to reach the highest level out of four.

The WMO said there was an “exceptionally high likelihood of nearly 100 percent” that El Nino will continue through to February.

El Nino can reshape weather and climate patterns thousands of kilometres away from the tropical Pacific.

Every El Nino is different, but major events often follow familiar patterns. This includes drought across parts of the Amazon, Indonesia and Australia, disrupted monsoons in India and shifting rainfall throughout the tropics.

For September-November, WMO forecasts indicate an increased likelihood of above-normal temperatures “across almost all land areas”, alongside rainfall patterns showing a “pronounced and classic atmospheric response to the strong Pacific El Nino”, the weather agency said.

The index, which measures sea surface temperature anomalies in the central eastern equatorial Pacific, has strengthened from an average 1.5C (2.7F) above normal between May and July.

Weekly values between late July and mid-August ranged from 2.2C to 2.6C (4F to 4.7F) above average, indicating continued El Nino intensification.

In some areas, subsurface ocean temperatures were more than 8C (14.4F) above average during July and early August.

articles.title: College lecturer admits killing husband and wife in drink-drive crash
articles.summary: Sophie Hynd caused the deaths of Jatinder Kaur, 48, and Satwant Singh, 64, in Cluny, Fife, in December last year.
articles.body:
A former college lecturer has admitted killing a husband and wife in a head-on crash while drink-driving after a work Christmas party.

Sophie Hynd caused the deaths of Jatinder Kaur, 48, and her husband Satwant Singh, 64, on the B981 in Cluny, Fife, on December 19 last year .

The couple's 10-year-old son was also seriously injured in the incident.

Hynd, 33, who lost her job teaching computer animation at Fife College, wept as she was remanded in custody at the High Court in Edinburgh.

Judge Michael O'Grady KC described the offence as "very grave".

The family said they were still coming to terms with the "devastating loss".

More stories from Edinburgh, Fife & East

The court heard that the crash happened following Christmas lunch and drinks on on the last day of the college term.

Hynd, from Kirkcaldy, had been drinking alcohol including cider, spritz, Prosecco and possibly a Guinness shot.

She left to go home at about 22:30 and was seen to be unsteady on her feet.

Advocate depute Lynsey Rodger said: "The accused was described as 'pretty merry' by one colleague and 'pretty drunk' by another."

Drivers called 999 after seeing Hynd's Nissan Qashqai moving erratically and swerving into the opposing carriageway.

At the time Jatinder Kaur was driving the family's Volkswagen Polo, making deliveries with her husband and their children in the car.

The family ran the Keystore grocery store in Kirkcaldy.

The couple's 19-year-old daughter Parveet was in the front passenger seat and their son Princedeep, 10, was sleeping in the back seat beside his father.

The advocate depute added: "The accused's vehicle crashed head-on, which caused both vehicles to come to a stop."

Other drivers who witnessed Hynd's erratic driving stopped to try and help, with police and paramedics arriving a short time later.

Rodger said that at the scene police observed that Hynd "smelled of alcohol and appeared to not know she had been in a collision".

Kaur was unresponsive and was pronounced dead at the scene. Satwant Singh was taken to hospital where he died two days later.

Hynd was arrested and charged in May this year.

Defence lawyer Ewen Roy said that she recognised that her actions had "devastating consequences which weigh on her heavily".

Judge O'Grady told Hynd: "You understand the charge you have pled guilty to is very grave indeed.

"You have left in your wake a dead husband and wife."

In a statement, the family said "we will miss them more than words can express".

They added: "Mum was always there for us, whether we needed her advice, reassurance or someone to talk to, she always made things better.

"Nothing was ever too much trouble for Dad, he loved Mum and us more than anything.

"It's incredibly difficult to accept they won't be there to share the important milestones in our lives."

The case is due to call again in October.

articles.title: Man rescued from inside garbage truck in San Francisco
articles.summary: A man was rescued from inside a garbage truck Wednesday morning in San Francisco, according to the fire department.
articles.body: A man was rescued from inside a garbage truck Wednesday morning in San Francisco, according to the fire department. Firefighters were dispatched around 4:11 a.m. to the 100 block of Mason Street following a report of a person trapped inside a Recology garbage truck. According to SFFD, the truck’s driver had been flagged down and told that someone could be heard yelling from inside the garbage area of the truck. About 25 firefighters responded to the scene, and the rescue operation took roughly two hours, according to fire officials. The man was eventually rescued and was conscious, breathing and talking before being taken to a hospital, according to a San Francisco Fire Department spokesperson. The extent of his injuries was not immediately known. A firefighter also suffered a laceration to the hand during the rescue and was taken to a hospital for stitches, fire officials added. A fire official said he is believed to have entered a dumpster looking for food before he got trapped in the garbage truck.

articles.title: Russia will close German cultural centers after Berlin blames Moscow for airport drone plot
articles.summary: Russia will shutter German cultural centers across the country, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Thursday, in a tit-for-tat measure that reflected soured relations and deepening tensions.
articles.body: WARSAW, Poland — Russia will shutter German cultural centers across the country, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Thursday, in a tit-for-tat measure that reflected soured relations and deepening tensions between Moscow and European countries helping Ukraine resist Russia’s invasion. Lavrov’s announcement came after Berlin blamed Moscow for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport. Germany said Wednesday it was consequently closing both the Russian Consulate in Bonn and the Russian House cultural center in the German capital. Western officials have repeatedly accused Moscow of running a campaign of sabotage and disruption in their countries with the aim of undermining support for Ukraine and destabilizing European nations, something Russian officials deny. Europe increasingly views itself as facing what it calls a hybrid war with Russia, marked by tools such as cyberwarfare and disinformation as well as a conventional military threat. Each side accuses the other of state terrorism. The tension has continued for months and grown into one of the greatest foreign and defense policy challenges for countries in the European Union. Russian President Vladimir Putin is testing the West with tactics that fall “just below the threshold of war” and is determined to “harass NATO members,” the head of Britain’s MI6 spy agency said at the end of last year. European countries take steps to counter Russia’s threat The British government summoned the top Russian diplomat in London on Thursday to protest what it called Russia’s “egregious and reckless attack” on the German airport last month. The U.K. government called the incident the “latest in a clear pattern of attempts by Russia” to undermine European security. In Finland on Thursday, more than 2,000 people took part in the biggest civil defense exercise in Europe since the end of World War II. Among the threats envisaged were missile strikes from neighboring Russia. Meanwhile, Norwegian authorities seized a Russian vessel in the Arctic archipelago of Svalbard on Wednesday at the request of Ukraine’s Naftogaz. The seizure was part of a global effort to enforce a $4.22 billion arbitration award and comes after a European push to seize vessels belonging to Russia’s so-called shadow fleet, which officials say contravenes international sanctions. Russia says German cultural presence is over Lavrov said that cultural centers belonging to Germany’s Goethe-Institut would be closed in Moscow, St. Petersburg and Yekaterinburg, adding that any other response would show a lack of “self-respect” on Russia’s part. Speaking at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, Lavrov said that Germany “could not have failed to understand” that the closure of Russian House would “signify the end of their cultural presence in Russia.” A drone laden with explosives was found near a Ukrainian plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 4 and later defused. The airport is a major international freight hub used for providing support to Ukraine. Putin has dismissed the allegations, saying Berlin wants to distract from its own failings and dissatisfaction among voters. Any proof being offered “has been planted,” Putin said. EU working on response after attempted Russian attack European Union ministers on Wednesday weighed how best to respond to the attempted drone attack but struggled to find new ways to meet the challenge without resorting to military means. The EU has slapped almost two dozen packages of sanctions on Russia over the war in Ukraine, hitting more than 3,000 officials, oligarchs and entities including banks, energy companies and drone makers. Germany insisted it was “not at war” but had become a “daily target” of the Kremlin’s hybrid campaign. Putin dismissed the allegations, saying Berlin aims to distract from its own failings and dissatisfaction among voters. Any proof being offered “has been planted,” Putin said. Denmark sounds alarm about Russian sabotage plans Danish security services are warning that Russian acts of sabotage against the country’s defense industry may be imminent. Danish intelligence services have seen signs of very specific planning by Russia to conduct sabotage operations in the country, Emil Græsholm, head of counterintelligence at the Danish national security and intelligence service PET, told the Berlingske newspaper. The targets are primarily companies in the defense industry and especially those associated with delivering military components to Ukraine, he said. Italy’s Defense Minister Guido Crosetto told The Associated Press on Wednesday that the Leipzig/Halle Airport incident was “a very serious act that could have very grave consequences.” But he said the threats aren’t discouraging Italy from providing further help to Kyiv as Rome weighs whether to send SAMP/T air defense batteries. As in other Western countries, limited weapons production capacity is hampering efforts to supply more to Ukraine, he said.

articles.title: Why has the Netherlands moved $10bn of its gold from the US?
articles.summary: The Netherlands has $83.7bn worth of gold in domestic and foreign reserves.
articles.body:
The Netherlands has moved billions of dollars of its gold reserves out of the United States and Canada, and transferred them to the United Kingdom amid global geopolitical tensions.

On Wednesday, the Dutch Central Bank (DNB) said it had moved the gold reserves to ensure it is “better prepared for severe crises”.

While DNB did not specify which crises it might need to be prepared for, the US is currently engaged in a bitter trade tariff war with Canada, while Washington is conducting a war in Iran and has led operations in Venezuela and around Cuba in recent months.

Furthermore, tensions between Europe and the US have risen since the start of the US war on Iran in February this year, as Trump has made his displeasure at the reluctance of European allies to join the war known.

In a statement, DNB President Olaf Sleijpen said: “With this relocation, we have improved the tradability of our gold reserves. We expect that we will never need to use them, but we do need to strengthen our resilience and preparedness.”

How many gold reserves does the Netherlands have? What does this mean for the US?

How much does the Netherlands have in gold reserves?

The Netherlands holds 612.4 tonnes of gold, valued at approximately 72.2 billion euros ($83.8bn), in gold reserves. These can serve as security in times of potential crises, where regular financial systems could fail.

As part of their standard risk diversification strategies, countries tend to spread their gold reserves around different locations to ensure the greatest security.

DNB spreads these gold reserves across different locations, including its own Cash Centre in Zeist, as well as in central banks in the UK, US and Canada.

Up until now, Zeist held 30.8 percent of the Netherlands’ gold reserves; London held 18.1 percent; New York, 31.3 percent; and Ottawa, 19.7 percent.

Following relocation of gold reserves from North America to the UK, the spread is now as follows: Zeist, 30.8 percent; London, 32.1 percent; New York, 18.5 percent; and Ottowa, 18.5 percent.

The relocated gold was valued at about 10.11 billion euros ($11.73bn) at the end of 2025. This was estimated at 10.34 billion euros as of 3pm (13:00 GMT) on Wednesday in the Netherlands.

It was moved in two ways: By selling gold in one location and buying it in another; and by physically transporting gold bars from one place to another.

According to DNB, the transfer of gold reserves began with the bank first selling about 59 tonnes of gold (worth about $8.3bn) in New York and then buying gold in London.

“More than 27 tonnes of gold (approximately $3.84bn) was also physically transferred from the United States and Canada to Zeist, and a similar quantity of gold that meets the international market standards was transferred from Zeist to London, preventing the need to remelt gold bars,” the bank said.

In all, about $10.7bn in gold has been moved from New York, while a little more than $1bn has been shifted from Ottawa, at the December 2025 valuations.

“Following the recent relocation, the geographical spread of the Dutch gold reserves is now more balanced, with both the United States and Canada each holding 18.5 percent,” DNB added.

Why did the Netherlands move this gold in this way?

According to DNB, the decision to move gold – and to do so in two ways – is part of its risk diversification strategy.

It stated: “Combining the processes of buying and selling and physical transport has allowed DNB to spread the risks associated with such a complex physical gold relocation operation, while also ensuring efficiency and cost-consciousness.

“Moreover, experience of both approaches will be useful in the event that another relocation is required during a potential future crisis, and one of the two approaches proves impossible due to circumstances at the time. This also fits in with DNB’s efforts to increase its crisis preparedness.”

Why might the Netherlands be moving gold away from the US?

In its press statement on Tuesday, DNB said it is seeking to ensure its gold is “easily tradeable” and highlighted that it considers London a safe place to keep it.

“Keeping a larger share of the gold reserves in London strengthens the function of gold as an anchor of trust. Gold is seen as the ultimate reserve asset because it is ideally suited to hedge extreme systemic risks,” DNB said.

“The gold reserves held in New York and Ottawa cannot be utilised as quickly and directly in such a situation,” the bank stated.

DNB has not explained what “systemic risks” it might be hedging against.

However, the Netherlands has removed far more gold from the US than it has from Canada, and analysts speculate there may be a number of reasons to fear instability in transatlantic relations.

Laurent Schwartz, president of the Paris-based National Gold Counter, a trading facility, told the UK’s Guardian newspaper: “The current political context in the United States might also push certain central banks into favouring other storage locations.”

First, Canada and the US have been locked in a trade war since 2025. The Trump administration hit Ottawa with tariffs on its key sectors of steel, aluminium and automobiles last year. Then, in August this year, Washington imposed an additional 50 percent tariff on $20bn of Canadian goods after trade talks between the two countries failed to yield an agreement.

In response, Ottawa unveiled retaliatory measures , levying tariffs against more than 700 US products, also valued at $20bn. These tariffs are tiered at 15, 25 and 50 percent, and are slated to come into effect on September 8.

Second, besides the various trade wars the Trump administration has been engaged in during President Donald Trump’s second term in the White House, the US-Israel war on Iran is ongoing – with no diplomatic or military end in sight – and Washington has also ramped up military operations around Cuba .

In January, US forces abducted Venezuela’s then-President Nicolas Maduro in a lightning military operation and transported him to the US to stand trial on drugs-and-guns charges. Since then, the US has struck deals to take control of a large part of Venezuela’s oil industry.

Third, diplomatic relations between European countries and the Trump administration have become more strained both as a result of the US’s trade wars and Trump’s anger that European nations have refused to join the war against Iran.

Last year, tempers between the US and Europe flared when Trump reiterated his ambitions to acquire Greenland and threatened European countries that got in his way with more trade tariffs.

In April this year, Trump ranted at European countries, telling them to “go get your own oil” from the Gulf, where the war has caused the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, triggering oil and gas shortages and chaos in world energy markets.

“All of those countries that can’t get jet fuel because of the strait of Hormuz, like the United Kingdom, which refused to get involved in the decapitation of Iran”, should buy US oil instead, Trump wrote on social media.

His comments followed news that France had barred Israeli planes from flying weapons through its airspace and Italy had refused permission for US bombers to land in Sicily. Spain refused permission for the US to use its bases and airspace for the war on Iran and, while the UK did allow the US to use its bases, then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer told parliament that the UK would not get involved in the war. Trump responded that the UK-US “relationship is obviously not what it was”.

Fourth, when the European Union first froze approximately $300bn of Russian central bank sovereign assets in February 2022 just days after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, many saw this as a new precedent.

While central banks have long had the ability to freeze the assets they hold belonging to other nations, they have rarely done so – and not on this scale. The frozen assets represented around half of Russia’s total $640bn wealth. By targeting a G20 super economy, the EU broke with a long-held tradition that the reserves of a major nuclear and economic power were out of bounds, under standard international financial norms.

The EU went a step further in 2024 when it and G7 nations agreed to a mechanism to utilise profits generated by these frozen assets for a $50bn loan package for Ukraine. Then, in December 2025, the bloc agreed make the freezing of Russian sovereign assets indefinite, thus removing the need to vote every six months on extending the asset freeze.

As a result, countries may begin calculating that it is high-risk to hold reserves with the central banks of other countries where the government or leaders are considered unpredictable.

Have other countries moved gold from the US?

The Netherlands is not the first country to move its gold reserves from the US this year.

In January, Banque de France moved 129 tonnes of gold, worth about $17bn, which had been held in the Federal Reserve Bank of New York since July 2025, back to France, citing a technical upgrade and seeking a better return as the reasons. To do this, the bank sold gold in New York and bought gold bars in Paris.

Between 2013 and 2017, Germany moved more than 600 tonnes of gold (worth about $77.5bn) from New York to Frankfurt to secure its national reserves, it said.

articles.title: Carla Jeffery, star of Disney Channel’s ‘Zombies,’ dies at 33
articles.summary: Carla Jeffery, best known for her role in the Disney Channel’s movie franchise “Zombies,” died age 33.
articles.body: Carla Jeffery, best known for her role in the Disney Channel movie franchise “Zombies,” died Tuesday. She was 33. Jeffery’s manager, Carla Alexander, shared the news in a post on the actor’s Instagram page Wednesday night. “It is with profound sadness that we share the passing of our beloved Carla Jeffery, who passed away on September 1, 2026, at just 33 years old,” the statement read. The post said that Jeffery joined the Alexanders Talent Management group when she was just 12. “For more than 20 years, we had the privilege of watching her grow into a beautiful, vibrant, and incredibly talented woman whose radiant smile could light up any room,” Alexander wrote in the statement. “Carla was more than a client; she was family.” Jeffery played cheerleader Bree in “Zombies,” according to the statement, and “shared her joy, humor, and bright spirit with audiences around the world.” The statement asked for privacy for Jeffery’s loved ones. Jeffery’s “Zombies” co-stars were swift to share tributes in the hours following the announcement. Marlo Manheim, who played Zed, posted pictures and videos of himself and Jeffery on his Instagram story. One was captioned, “Love you Carlaboo. The sweetest, kindest, most loving person.” Trevor Tordjman, who held the role of Bucky Buchanan, also posted tributes to Jeffery online. “Carla, you will be missed,” he wrote. “Will never forget your energy. Truly one of a kind.” Carlon Jeffrey, her brother who is also an actor, shared an image of his sister online and said she was “truly a light that shines bright.” He added, “You are the best sister a brother could ask for. Pray we continue to grow closer to one another along this journey. I got your back in this life and the next.” Jeffery held a number of roles on children’s television shows on the Disney Channel and Nickelodeon, including “iCarly,” “Good Luck Charlie” and “Shake It Up,” according to her IMDb page. She also appeared on 10 episodes of “Curb Your Enthusiasm.” Her breakout role was in “Zombies,” though, when she scored the role of Bree in the 2018 TV movie. She reprised the role in the second and third installments of the movie, and voiced the character in the animated version, “Zombies: The Re-Antimated Series.”

articles.title: It’s a top guest complaint but many hotels can’t fix it
articles.summary: As the importance of quality sleep becomes more widely known, hotel guests are insisting on peace and quiet. But tackling noise is challenging – and can be costly for hotels.
articles.body: On a work trip to Mississippi last year, Jason GaNun wound up trying three different hotel rooms to get some peace and quiet before a busy day — and none of them did the trick. In the first one, he said the “ancient” air conditioning unit was one of the loudest he’d ever encountered. When he moved to the second room, it was the refrigerator noise that got in the way of sleeping. And next to the third room he tried, other hotel guests were throwing a party. “I could hear everything they were doing,” said GaNun, a project manager for a demolition company in Pennsylvania who travels every other week for work. For Lindsey Maness, the menace during one hotel stay for work in Austin, Texas, was a noisy elevator near her room. Seven months pregnant at the time, Maness could hear the “dinging” of the elevators opening and closing all night. That wasn’t the only issue. “The walls were paper thin, and I could hear people in the room adjacent … chatting until very late in the night,” said Maness, who now works for the National Sleep Foundation. Far and away, it was “the worst night of sleep” she’s had at a hotel. Anyone who stays in hotels regularly has probably faced the same issue: Noise. External noise, internal noise, it doesn’t matter. After cleanliness, it’s the top concern of hotel guests, according to ProStay, a software and consulting firm that serves hotels. And with an increased emphasis on quality sleep for health and wellness, hotel guests are more adamant than ever that a good night’s sleep is a key part of what they’re booking. Yet tackling noise issues is challenging in part because the sources vary — think traffic on a busy street in Manhattan versus yelling in a neighboring room. Plus, sound mitigation sometimes entails costly build-outs or renovations. Here’s what’s at play — and what guests can do to protect their slumber. It’s what a hotel is for, isn’t it? While having a place to sleep has always been the primary solution guests are seeking from hotels, creating a calm, quiet environment hasn’t always been the predominant preoccupation of hoteliers, says Chekitan S. Dev, a professor at Cornell University’s Nolan School of Hotel Administration and a hospitality marketing and branding expert. “It wasn’t made a priority in a significant way by hotels until the late 90s,” Dev told CNN Travel. One manifestation of that shift is a Holiday Inn Express ad campaign that ran for more than a decade beginning in 1998 and showed ordinary people completing complex tasks such as brain surgery that were far outside their professional expertise. When asked if they were up to the job, they would explain it away by saying, “But I did stay at a Holiday Inn Express hotel last night.” But in many cases, hotels have invested more time and money in recent years in creating attractive lobbies, fine dining restaurants and exercise facilities. Yet as hotel prices climb, so do guests’ expectations, and in the end, guests need to sleep. “If you are charging me $400 a night for a hotel, I expect the room to be quiet,” Dev said. Simon Chapman, general manager of The Benjamin in New York City, says today’s travelers are much more attentive to “the quality of their sleep.” “They are no longer only asking whether a bed is comfortable; they are thinking about the complete environment — sound, light, room temperature, pillow support and how easily they can disconnect from technology,” he said in an email. The value of eight hours of sound sleep has become more apparent to guests in an era of meditation apps and wearable fitness trackers that monitor sleep. “The importance of sleep is becoming more front and center in everyday people’s lives for all of the work they have to do when they are in their regular living environment,” said John Lopos, CEO of the National Sleep Foundation. “And when they go out on the road, why should they sacrifice that?” What hotels can control There’s a lot that hotel owners can do to mitigate sound for all guests, particularly when they are building new properties. Lopos says “if there’s new construction, they should absolutely be thinking about things like sound mitigation … in the design and construction phase, including the selection of materials, what are they doing to manage sound, light and climate?” There are standards for sound transmission in modern building codes. According to Glenn Nowak, an associate professor of architecture at the University of Nevada at Las Vegas, a sound transmission class (STC) score of 50 is “the benchmark.” Hotels whose rooms are built with that sound score would render a normal conversation taking place in one room “inaudible” in an adjacent room and “loud music would be quite faint.” The problem? “Many hotels around the world were built before such standards were put in place,” Nowak told CNN Travel. And in newer properties, renovations sometimes inadvertently reduce a hotel’s sound rating. Whether the property is old or new, the main obstacle is often a financial one. All of these considerations aimed at mitigating sound cost money. “The tension is the investment required to create a good night’s sleep that is commensurate with the price point for the hotel room,” Dev of Cornell says. “Sometimes hotels don’t invest the amount that’s required.” And the acoustical properties of materials vary widely. Nowak says when you’re dealing with sound mitigation, a “cast-in-place concrete wall” is often “significantly superior to a metal stud frame wall.” But for the hotel, that translates into a bigger investment. “The concrete wall takes longer to build, is less flexible, and has higher labor costs,” he said. “A concrete wall is a lot heavier than a metal stud wall, so this design decision would impact the entire building’s structural system.” This is also true of building double walls, Nowak said, which are “among the more advanced strategies for … acoustically separating each room from the next,” but add to construction costs. Beyond the physical construction of a hotel, which may or may not have been built to mitigate sound, travelers also typically contend with reservation systems that don’t really allow them to choose rooms in specific areas that could be quieter. There are typically no schematics like airlines offer to allow travelers to choose their ideal situation — window or aisle, front or back. Unfortunately, you can’t see which hotel rooms are occupied or where they’re located. Frequent travelers like GaNun say rooms on higher floors or at the end of hallways are quieter. But even if a guest anticipates the problem and tries to find a solution such as booking a corner room, it’s not easy to do without talking to someone on site. Dev says it’s his pet peeve, and something he discusses often with hotel general managers and his students. “You can see every seat available on the plane,” he says, referring to online flight booking. “Why can’t I do the same when I book a hotel?” GaNun agrees. “Let me pick where I stay,” he said. Dev says some chains are looking into this shift in reservations but balancing housekeeping needs with a variety of arrival and departure times isn’t simple. There are also security concerns that keep hotels from displaying occupancy levels during the online reservation process. Some hotels are marketing their quietest rooms to travelers who are looking for an especially restorative sleep experience. Under the “sleep tourism” umbrella, they often come paired with amenities such as a choice of pillows or weighted sleep masks. But it all comes at a premium the average traveler is unlikely to pay for a routine hotel stay. Guests can, of course, call a hotel directly to ask for a quieter room at the end of a hall or far from the elevator, or put concerns over noise in the notes section of the online reservation system. Those requests can also be made at check-in, although the options narrow when occupancy is high. What hotels can’t control Exterior noise presents its own challenges. In New Orleans, it could be sudden bursts of sound from passing musicians. When Silvia Passiflora traveled to New Orleans, music coming from outside of her hotel room woke her up. A musician herself, Passiflora knows New Orleans is a hot spot for live music so it didn’t bother her that much. But the late-night revelry definitely penetrated the walls of her hotel. “I kept waking up at 2, 3, 4 in the morning to music,” she said. Sounds coming from the exterior often aren’t consistent, and hence they can be quite jarring for a traveler. The Benjamin, for example, is located at Lexington Avenue and 50th Street in Manhattan, a few blocks from Rockefeller Plaza and other popular tourist attractions. “No hotel — especially one in the heart of Manhattan — can eliminate every sound,” says Chapman, the general manager, adding, “City activity can be unpredictable.” Many urban properties like The Benjamin have invested in multi-pane windows, and blackout curtains, which can block both light and sound. In lieu of bigger changes that could reduce noise complaints, many hotels now routinely hand out earplugs and eye masks. And that’s helpful because some rooms — or areas of the hotel — are louder than others. Maness, who spent the night clocking the hotel elevator’s comings and goings, said her room was on the first floor where sounds often reverberate. She learned a lot from her lousy night in Texas. “I now request hotel rooms as far away from the elevator as possible and try to book rooms with no adjacent guests when possible,” Maness said. Chapman, the GM of The Benjamin, encourages such a request, saying guests can indicate “higher floor, quieter location, or room away from the elevator,” and if availability allows, their requests will be accommodated. Many large hotel chains also face another issue: they serve a wide swath of people with divergent needs, including business travelers gathering for a conference, couples on a romantic weekend getaway and families looking to entertain children. For this last group, what’s better than a hotel with a pool? When Marie Cloutier stayed at a budget-friendly hotel in Massachusetts during a conference, the hotel pool was located in a ground-floor atrium at the center of the property where everyone could see — and hear — it. She assumed, incorrectly, that the fun would wind down at night. “When I called the hotel manager, he said the kids needed their playtime and the rest of us could suck it up!” she said. Of course, some of the reasons guests struggle to sleep while traveling have nothing to do with the thickness of the walls or noise from the hallway. Lopos says especially with work travel, “You’re out of your routine, you’re socializing, it’s stressful.” Hotel guests often have an ill-advised nightcap in the lobby bar. They eat heavily right before bedding down for the night. They stay out later than usual. All of that affects sleep. How to up your chances of a restful stay Consumers are increasingly able to customize other products and services they buy. Could that one day mean an online reservation system that allows travelers to have greater control over the rooms they are assigned at hotels? Maybe. “The locus of control is shifting from the operator to the customer,” says Dev of Cornell. But it may take time for hotels to catch up to guests who increasingly view a solid night’s sleep as the most important amenity a hotel can offer but aren’t prepared to pay an arm and a leg for an exclusive sleep suite. In the meantime, hotel guests often have to find solutions on their own. In addition to requests for quieter, less occupied parts of a hotel, you can consult websites, including The Quiet Hotels and another similarly named Quiet Hotels, that give hotels scores based on how quiet they are. The Quiet Hotels, for example, gives ratings for hotels in New York, Atlanta, Los Angeles and many other cities. Hotels with scores of 90 or above are deemed “exceptionally quiet.” And the website explains its methodology. The editors evaluate the hotel’s surroundings for busy roads or nightlife and also assess the building’s construction, paying attention to sound transfer, window quality and room positioning. So for its entry on The Lowell in Manhattan, for example, the site’s authors say the hotel is on a residential block of East 63rd Street with no through traffic, plus there’s a “low room count over fourteen quiet floors.” Meanwhile, an entry for Boston, Hotel Commonwealth, cites the building’s “concrete-and-steel post-2003 construction with high-acoustic glass.” Guests can also book rooms that face an interior courtyard. Note that none of the hotels listed are budget properties, but some are moderately priced. Nowak, at UNLV, recommends older properties like The Peery Hotel in Salt Lake City, Utah, which was built in 1910 with “massive load-bearing brick walls” and appears on the National Register of Historic Places. General Manager Todd Wheeler says the “historic craftsmanship” that went into building the hotel helps make the property relaxing. “Many guests appreciate the sense of quiet that comes from the building’s solid masonry construction,” he said. Lopos encourages all travelers to embrace pro-sleep activities like getting a lot of natural light during the daytime, exercising and sticking to a consistent meal schedule. Closing the curtains tightly before bed and turning down the thermostat also help. Lopos also travels with a white noise machine wherever he goes, and hotels are increasingly outfitting rooms with updated alarm clocks that have a variety of sound settings. Hotel occupancy rates have been quite strong this year, with American properties reporting record levels, according to a report from CoStar and Tourism Economics. It’s good news for the travel sector, but for those hotel guests plagued by loud elevators and rowdy fellow guests, it may just sound noisy. So to be on the safe side, pack your earplugs.

articles.title: ‘Supersized’ El Nino could reshape global weather and push 2027 to heat record: UN
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A \"supersized\" El Nino could strengthen further into 2027 and potentially become the strongest such event ever recorded, raising the risk of extreme w.
articles.body: A "supersized" El Nino could strengthen further into 2027 and potentially become the strongest such event ever recorded, raising the risk of extreme weather including droughts, heavy rainfall and powerful tropical storms worldwide, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) warned on Thursday.The UN weather agency said there is an almost 100% probability that the phenomenon will persist through February 2027, driven by exceptionally warm temperatures in the Pacific Ocean. It said this was the first time it had expressed such a high level of confidence in El Nino's continued presence.“If this trajectory continues, it may be stronger than anything since our monitoring began. So literally off the charts,” WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo told reporters at a news conference in Geneva.El Nino is a recurring climate pattern caused by changes in ocean temperatures and trade winds in the tropical Pacific. It typically occurs every two to seven years and can last for up to 12 months, disrupting weather patterns across large parts of the world.A particularly strong El Nino can alter normal rainfall and temperature patterns, increasing the likelihood of severe droughts, flooding, heavy rainfall and powerful tropical storms. Its effects can also disrupt agriculture and food supplies, particularly in vulnerable regions.Warming Pacific raises concernThe WMO said Pacific Ocean temperatures linked to the current El Nino are already more than 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) above normal. The event is among only four classified as "very strong" in records dating back to 1950.Although El Nino is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon and is not directly caused by fossil fuel-driven climate change, rising global ocean temperatures can influence its intensity and amplify its impacts.“El Nino is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: The planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up,” UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said.The effects are already being felt across tropical regions, including through disruptions to soft commodity production. In Central America's Dry Corridor, El Nino-related weather conditions have contributed to a severe food crisis.2027 could see temperature recordThe WMO expects the current El Nino to peak towards the end of this year, but warned that its influence could extend into 2027 and contribute to elevated global temperatures, as per the Reuters.Wilfran Moufouma Okia, the WMO's chief of climate prediction services, said El Nino events are normally followed by a temporary increase in global temperatures.“Normally after an El Nino event we tend to see a pulse in global temperatures — a temporary one,” he said, referring to 2024, which was the hottest year on record so far. “2027 has the potential to be the warmest on record.”The potential for a record-strength El Nino has prompted the WMO to strengthen preparedness and early-warning measures to help governments anticipate its impacts.Such measures could include early shifts towards drought-resistant crops in vulnerable regions and preparedness across climate-sensitive sectors including agriculture, health, energy and water resources.“WMO is committed to working closely with partners across the United Nations and humanitarian system to provide the climate intelligence and insights needed to support disaster management and climate-sensitive sectors like agriculture, health, energy and water resources,” Saulo said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
